questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: The fundamental accounting equation underlying the balance sheet states that

answers.text: Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders' Equity
Revenues - Expenses = Net Income
Cash Inflows - Cash Outflows = Net Change in Cash
Beginning Equity + Net Income - Dividends = Ending Equity

explanations.a: The balance sheet equation (Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders' Equity) reflects that every asset owned by the entity is financed either through obligations to creditors (liabilities) or through the owners' investment and retained earnings (stockholders' equity). This equation must remain in balance at all times and is the foundation of double-entry bookkeeping.
explanations.b: Revenues minus expenses equal net income — this is the income statement relationship, not the balance sheet equation.
explanations.c: Cash inflows minus cash outflows equal the net change in cash — this is the cash flow statement relationship, not the balance sheet equation.
explanations.d: Beginning equity plus net income minus dividends equals ending equity — this is the retained earnings rollforward, a component of the statement of changes in equity, not the fundamental balance sheet equation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: Under US GAAP, an asset is classified as current on the balance sheet when

answers.text: It is expected to be converted to cash, sold, or consumed within one year or within the entity's operating cycle, whichever is longer
Management intends to convert the asset to cash within the next fiscal year, regardless of ability
It is expected to be converted to cash or consumed within exactly 12 months — the operating cycle is irrelevant for US GAAP current asset classification
The asset's fair value exceeds its book value at the balance sheet date

explanations.a: ASC 210-10-45 defines current assets as cash and other assets expected to be converted to cash, sold, or consumed within one year or within the normal operating cycle of the business, whichever is longer. The operating cycle is the time between cash outlays for inventory and the collection of cash from resulting sales.
explanations.b: Management intent alone does not determine current classification — the ability to convert and the expected conversion timeframe are the operative criteria. Assets cannot be reclassified as current simply because management wishes to liquidate them.
explanations.c: The one-year rule alone is insufficient — US GAAP (ASC 210) uses the longer of one year or the operating cycle. Industries with long operating cycles (such as tobacco aging or whiskey distillation) may classify assets as current even if conversion takes longer than 12 months.
explanations.d: The relationship between fair value and book value determines whether impairment exists — it has no bearing on whether an asset is classified as current or non-current.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: At December 31, a company's long-term debt agreement contains a covenant requiring the company to maintain a debt-to-equity ratio below 2.0. At year-end the ratio is 2.4, and the lender has not granted a waiver. How should this debt be classified on the December 31 balance sheet?

answers.text: As a current liability — the covenant violation gives the lender the right to call the debt immediately, making it due on demand and therefore current
As a non-current liability — covenant violations do not affect balance sheet classification; only the stated maturity date determines classification
As a non-current liability with footnote disclosure of the covenant violation — disclosure without reclassification is sufficient
Excluded from the balance sheet entirely pending resolution of the covenant violation

explanations.a: ASC 470-10-45 requires that when a debt covenant is violated and the lender has the right to demand immediate payment — and has not waived that right as of the balance sheet date — the debt is reclassified as current. The right of the creditor to accelerate the debt makes it effectively due on demand, which requires current presentation regardless of the original stated maturity.
explanations.b: The stated maturity date does not control classification when a covenant violation has given the lender acceleration rights. If the lender can demand immediate repayment, the debt is current regardless of when it was originally scheduled to mature.
explanations.c: Footnote disclosure alone is insufficient when reclassification is required. While disclosure of covenant violations is required, the accounting treatment also requires reclassification to current liabilities when the creditor has the right to demand payment and has not waived it.
explanations.d: Debt is not removed from the balance sheet due to covenant violations — it remains a liability that must be properly classified and disclosed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: A company maintains a compensating balance of $100,000 with its bank that is legally restricted from use for current obligations and will remain restricted for 18 months. Where should the $100,000 be presented on the balance sheet?

answers.text: As part of Cash and Cash Equivalents in current assets — all bank account balances are included in cash
As a current asset — compensating balances are always classified as current regardless of restrictions
As a non-current asset, separately labeled as 'Restricted Cash' or similar — since the restriction extends beyond one year and the cash is not available for current use
Netted against the related current liability to show the net obligation

explanations.a: Not all bank account balances qualify as 'Cash and Cash Equivalents.' Cash that is legally restricted and not available for general use within the current period must be excluded from the cash line item and presented separately.
explanations.b: Compensating balances subject to legal restrictions that extend beyond one year do not qualify as current assets. ASC 210 requires classification based on availability for use — a legally restricted balance unavailable for 18 months is non-current.
explanations.c: ASC 210-10-45 requires that restricted cash legally restricted from use for current obligations be classified outside of current assets. Since the restriction extends 18 months (beyond the one-year current asset threshold), the $100,000 should be presented as a non-current asset separately labeled (e.g., 'Restricted Cash' or 'Other Assets') rather than included in Cash and Cash Equivalents.
explanations.d: Offsetting is generally prohibited under ASC 210-20 — the restricted cash may not be netted against the related borrowing. It must be presented as an asset separately from the liability.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: A company receives a $600,000 advance payment from a customer in December for services to be provided equally over the following 24 months. On the December 31 balance sheet, the deferred revenue should be classified as

answers.text: $300,000 current (services to be provided in Year 1) and $300,000 non-current (services to be provided in Year 2)
Entirely current — advance payments from customers are always classified as current liabilities
Entirely non-current — since the full service period extends 24 months beyond December 31
Not a liability — advance payments become revenue when received

explanations.a: Deferred revenue represents an obligation to provide services in the future. Under ASC 210, the current portion of any liability is that which will be settled within one year. Since services are provided equally over 24 months, half ($300,000) will be earned in Year 1 (current) and half ($300,000) will be earned in Year 2 (non-current). This split presentation properly reflects the entity's obligation timeline.
explanations.b: Not all deferred revenue is automatically current — the current/non-current split depends on when the performance obligation will be satisfied. Only the portion expected to be earned within the next 12 months is current.
explanations.c: Classifying the entire $600,000 as non-current would overstate long-term obligations — $300,000 will be earned within 12 months, making it a current liability.
explanations.d: Advance payments create a liability (deferred revenue or contract liability under ASC 606) when the performance obligation has not yet been satisfied. Revenue is recognized as services are performed — not when cash is received.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: Under ASC 210-20, an entity may offset a financial asset and financial liability and present a net amount on the balance sheet ONLY when

answers.text: The entity has a legally enforceable right to offset the recognized amounts AND intends either to settle on a net basis or to simultaneously realize the asset and settle the liability
Both the asset and the liability are with the same counterparty — the same-counterparty condition alone is sufficient to permit offsetting
The entity's management believes that presenting net amounts provides more useful information to financial statement users
The asset and liability are denominated in the same currency and mature on the same date

explanations.a: ASC 210-20-45-1 establishes a two-condition test for offsetting: (1) the reporting entity has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognized amounts — meaning the right to offset must be enforceable at law, not merely a management intention; AND (2) the entity intends either to settle the amount net or to realize the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Both conditions must be met. A right of offset without intention to use it does not justify net presentation.
explanations.b: Being with the same counterparty is relevant context but is not sufficient alone. Many entities have receivables and payables with the same counterparty that cannot be offset — for example, trade receivables and trade payables with the same vendor/customer typically cannot be offset because there is no legally enforceable right to do so absent a specific netting agreement.
explanations.c: Management's belief about usefulness does not override the specific recognition criteria for offsetting. Presentation choices are governed by GAAP requirements, not by management's view of what is most informative.
explanations.d: Same currency and same maturity are characteristics of potentially offsettable instruments but are not the GAAP test. The legally enforceable right and settlement intention criteria are the operative requirements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: At December 31, Year 1, a company has long-term debt of $5 million with a stated maturity of Year 7. During Year 1, the company violated a debt covenant. On January 20, Year 2 — before the financial statements are issued — the lender signed a waiver agreement that cures the violation and waives the lender's right to demand payment for at least 12 months. How should the debt be classified on the December 31, Year 1 balance sheet?

answers.text: Non-current — the waiver agreement executed before the financial statements are issued restores non-current classification as of December 31, Year 1
Non-current — the original stated maturity of Year 7 always controls balance sheet classification regardless of covenant violations

Current — the waiver was not in place as of December 31, Year 1; the violation existed at year-end giving the lender acceleration rights, and the post-balance-sheet waiver does not retroactively restore non-current classification
The debt is excluded from the balance sheet and disclosed only in footnotes pending resolution of the covenant violation

explanations.a: This reverses the correct analysis. Under ASC 470-10-45-11, a waiver agreement executed after the balance sheet date but before financial statement issuance does NOT restore non-current classification. The exception applies only to waivers executed ON OR BEFORE the balance sheet date. A post-balance-sheet waiver is a subsequent event that does not change the balance sheet classification — though it may be disclosed as a subsequent event.
explanations.b: The stated maturity does not control when the creditor has obtained acceleration rights through a covenant violation. ASC 470-10-45 requires current classification when acceleration rights exist and have not been validly waived as of the balance sheet date.
explanations.c: ASC 470-10-45-11 requires the debt to be classified as current when a covenant violation exists at the balance sheet date and the lender has the right to demand payment — unless a waiver agreement effective for at least 12 months is executed ON OR BEFORE the balance sheet date. A waiver executed on January 20, Year 2 is after December 31, Year 1. Therefore, the debt must be classified as current on the Year 1 balance sheet, with the waiver disclosed as a subsequent event that may affect future classification.
explanations.d: Debt subject to covenant violations remains on the balance sheet — it is reclassified to current, not removed. Footnote disclosure of the covenant violation and subsequent waiver is required in addition to the reclassification.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: balance sheet and statement of financial position
questions.text: A company repurchases 10,000 shares of its own $1 par common stock at $25 per share, recording treasury stock using the cost method. The shares are held in the treasury — not retired. How does this transaction affect the balance sheet?

answers.text: Cash decreases by $250,000 and an asset 'Treasury Stock' increases by $250,000 — the repurchased shares are an asset since the company could sell them
Cash decreases by $250,000, common stock decreases by $10,000, and retained earnings decreases by $240,000
Cash decreases by $250,000 and total stockholders' equity decreases by $250,000 — treasury stock is recorded as a contra-equity deduction at cost
Cash decreases by $250,000 and retained earnings decreases by $250,000

explanations.a: Treasury stock is not an asset — an entity cannot own itself. A company's own shares held in treasury represent an equity reduction, not an investment. ASC 505-30 requires treasury stock to be classified as a reduction from stockholders' equity, not as an asset.
explanations.b: Under the cost method, the repurchase transaction records the full cost of repurchase in the treasury stock account — it does not separately affect common stock or retained earnings at the time of repurchase (those accounts may be affected when shares are retired or reissued at different amounts).
explanations.c: Under the cost method (ASC 505-30), treasury stock is debited at cost ($250,000) and is presented as a deduction from total stockholders' equity. Cash decreases by $250,000, and the treasury stock account (contra-equity) increases by $250,000, reducing total stockholders' equity by $250,000. Common stock and APIC are unchanged at the time of repurchase.
explanations.d: Treasury stock under the cost method is debited to a separate treasury stock account, not directly to retained earnings. Retained earnings is only affected when treasury shares are retired or reissued below cost (under certain methods).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: Under ASC 230-10, a component of an entity qualifies for discontinued operations presentation when

answers.text: Any segment or division of the entity ceases operations during the year, regardless of materiality

The disposal of the component represents a strategic shift that has or will have a major effect on an entity's operations and financial results — such as disposal of a major line of business or geographic area
The component has operated at a loss for three consecutive years — recurring losses automatically trigger discontinued operations classification
Management decides to discontinue the component at any point during the reporting period, even if no active disposal plan exists

explanations.a: Not every component that ceases operations qualifies for discontinued operations treatment — the disposal must represent a strategic shift with major effect on operations. Small or routine disposals do not meet the discontinued operations criteria under ASC 205-20.
explanations.b: ASC 205-20-45-1 requires two conditions for discontinued operations: (1) the component has been disposed of or classified as held for sale, and (2) the disposal represents a strategic shift that has or will have a major effect on the entity's operations and financial results — for example, a major line of business, a major geographical area, or a major equity method investment. This is the correct standard.
explanations.c: Operating losses alone do not qualify a component for discontinued operations treatment. The key criteria are the strategic shift and major effect on operations — financial performance is not a qualifying criterion.
explanations.d: A formal plan to sell and active marketing of the component are among the criteria for held-for-sale classification. Management simply deciding internally to discontinue an operation, without meeting the held-for-sale criteria, does not trigger discontinued operations presentation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: A company reports pre-tax income from continuing operations of $800,000 and a pre-tax loss from a discontinued operation of $300,000. The effective income tax rate is 25% applied to both. How should these amounts be presented on the income statement?

answers.text: A single net income figure of $375,000 [(($800,000 - $300,000) × 75%)] with supporting details in the footnotes

Income from continuing operations: $600,000 (net of $200,000 income tax expense); Loss from discontinued operation: $(225,000) (net of $75,000 tax benefit); presented separately, each net of its own tax effect
Income from continuing operations: $800,000 (gross, pre-tax); then a combined income tax expense of $125,000 applied to both items together; net income of $375,000
Income from continuing operations: $800,000; Loss from discontinued operation: $(300,000); combined income tax expense: $125,000; net income: $375,000

explanations.a: Combining the continuing and discontinued results into a single net income figure without separate presentation does not comply with ASC 205-20, which requires discontinued operations to be shown separately from continuing operations.
explanations.b: ASC 205-20-45 requires the results of discontinued operations to be presented separately from continuing operations on the income statement, with each amount shown net of its applicable income tax effect. Continuing operations: $800,000 pre-tax × 75% = $600,000. Discontinued operations: ($300,000) pre-tax × 75% = ($225,000) — shown separately below continuing operations with the label 'Loss from discontinued operation, net of tax benefit of $75,000.' This presentation allows users to assess the earnings power from ongoing operations independently of one-time disposal effects.
explanations.c: The tax expense must be allocated between continuing and discontinued operations — it cannot be applied only to the combined total below the discontinued operations line. Also, the discontinued operation must be shown net of tax, not gross.
explanations.d: Showing both continuing and discontinued operations gross (pre-tax) and then applying a single combined tax is not the prescribed presentation. Each category must be presented net of its own tax effect.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: Company A includes freight-out (shipping costs on goods sold to customers) in cost of goods sold. Company B reports the same type of freight-out costs as a separate selling expense line below gross profit. Under US GAAP

answers.text: Company A's classification is incorrect — freight-out must be included in selling expenses, not cost of goods sold
Company B's classification is incorrect — freight-out is a product cost that must always be included in cost of goods sold
Company A's presentation results in a higher gross profit than Company B's for identical economics

Both classifications are acceptable — US GAAP does not prescribe the classification of freight-out; the key requirement is consistent application and adequate disclosure when classification affects comparability

explanations.a: US GAAP (ASC 330 and related guidance) does not mandate a specific income statement classification for freight-out costs. Both cost of goods sold and selling expense classifications are widely used in practice and are acceptable.
explanations.b: Similarly, there is no requirement that freight-out be classified in cost of goods sold. Some companies view it as a fulfillment cost (product cost) and include it in COGS; others view it as a selling cost and present it below gross profit.
explanations.c: If Company A includes freight-out in COGS while Company B excludes it from COGS, Company A's gross profit would be LOWER (higher COGS), not higher — the question reverses the relationship. Including more costs in COGS reduces gross profit relative to classifying them below the gross profit line.
explanations.d: US GAAP provides flexibility in income statement classification for many expense items, including freight-out. The key principles are: (1) consistent application from period to period; (2) clear presentation so users can understand the classification; and (3) adequate disclosure when a company's classification differs from industry practice or when a change in classification occurs, so comparability across periods is transparent.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: A company's consumer products segment meets the held-for-sale criteria under ASC 205-20 on June 30. The segment is sold on October 15. For the annual income statement, which period's operations should be presented as discontinued?

answers.text: Only the period from July 1 through October 15 when the segment was classified as held for sale — results before July 1 remain in continuing operations
Only the period from October 15 (the sale date) through year-end — only post-disposal periods qualify as discontinued
None — since the segment was sold before year-end, it is presented entirely in continuing operations for the annual period

The entire year's results for the discontinued segment — all periods presented are reclassified to discontinued operations, including results from January through June, to provide users with a complete discontinued operations history

explanations.a: Only presenting results from July 1 onward would provide an incomplete picture of the discontinued segment's performance. ASC 205-20 requires retrospective reclassification of all periods presented so users can assess the entity's performance from continuing operations without the discontinued component in any period.
explanations.b: Discontinued operations presentation covers all periods presented in the financial statements — not only the period after the sale date. The segment's results for all prior periods presented are reclassified.
explanations.c: The sale before year-end does not eliminate discontinued operations presentation — it still qualifies because it met the held-for-sale criteria and represents a qualifying strategic shift. Disposal before year-end does not revert the classification to continuing operations.
explanations.d: ASC 205-20-45-10 requires that when a component is classified as a discontinued operation, all periods presented in the comparative financial statements are reclassified to show the discontinued component's results separately — including the pre-held-for-sale periods. This allows users to understand the continuing operations' performance in all comparative periods without the discontinued segment's activity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: In a multi-step income statement, which of the following items typically appears BELOW 'income from operations' (operating income)?

answers.text: Cost of goods sold — a primary deduction from revenues in calculating gross profit
Selling, general, and administrative expenses — deducted from gross profit to arrive at operating income
Depreciation of manufacturing equipment — a product cost included in cost of goods sold
Interest expense and income tax expense — non-operating items presented below operating income in a multi-step format

explanations.a: Cost of goods sold is deducted from net revenues to arrive at gross profit — it appears in the first section of the multi-step income statement, well above operating income.
explanations.b: SG&A expenses are operating expenses deducted from gross profit to arrive at income from operations — they appear above operating income, not below it.
explanations.c: Depreciation of manufacturing equipment is a product cost included in the overhead component of cost of goods sold — it is absorbed into inventory and eventually flows through COGS, which appears above operating income.
explanations.d: In a multi-step income statement, items below income from operations (operating income) include: interest income and expense (financing-related); gains and losses on investment transactions; and income tax expense. The structure separates operating performance from financing costs and taxes, allowing users to assess the core operating profitability of the business independently of its capital structure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: A company sells its entire Northern European distribution subsidiary, which had been a separately identifiable component with its own operations and cash flows, and the disposal represents a major strategic shift away from European markets. The subsidiary was carried at a net book value of $4 million and was sold for $5.5 million. How is the $1.5 million gain presented on the income statement?

answers.text: As a gain from continuing operations — gains on asset sales are always presented in continuing operations
Separately disclosed as an 'unusual item' within continuing operations
Amortized over 5 years as a deferred gain using the installment method
Within discontinued operations — the gain on disposal is included in the results of the discontinued component presented net of tax below continuing operations

explanations.a: The gain on disposal of a subsidiary that qualifies as a discontinued operation under ASC 205-20 is not presented in continuing operations. The entire discontinued component — including both its operating results and the gain or loss on disposal — is presented in the discontinued operations section.
explanations.b: 'Unusual items' as a separate category within continuing operations was eliminated by ASU 2015-01. Infrequent or unusual items are no longer separately classified within continuing operations — unusual or infrequent items that do not qualify as discontinued operations are simply included in income from continuing operations without separate classification.
explanations.c: The installment method for gain deferral (ASC 932 for certain industries) is not applicable here. Gains on disposal of subsidiaries are generally recognized at the point of sale, not deferred and amortized.
explanations.d: ASC 205-20-45-3 requires that when a component qualifies as a discontinued operation, the gain or loss on disposal is included within the discontinued operations section, presented net of income taxes. The $1.5 million gain (net of applicable taxes) is presented in the 'results of discontinued operations' line below income from continuing operations, providing users with a complete picture of the discontinued component's total financial impact.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: A company has 1,000,000 weighted-average shares outstanding for the year. It reports a loss from continuing operations of $(500,000) and a gain from discontinued operations of $800,000. For earnings per share (EPS) purposes, which presentation is required?

answers.text: A single EPS figure of $0.30 per share based on net income of $300,000 — only total net income EPS is required
EPS from continuing operations: $(0.50) per share; EPS from discontinued operations: $0.80 per share; presented separately on the face of the income statement — with the total EPS shown as well
EPS is not presented when there is a loss from continuing operations — EPS becomes antidilutive
Only EPS from continuing operations is required — discontinued operations EPS is disclosed only in footnotes

explanations.a: A single EPS figure for total net income does not comply with ASC 260. When discontinued operations exist, EPS must be disclosed for both continuing operations and discontinued operations separately — not just in aggregate.
explanations.b: ASC 260-10-45-3 requires that when a company presents discontinued operations, EPS amounts must be presented for: (1) income from continuing operations; (2) discontinued operations; and (3) net income — all on the face of the income statement or in the notes. This allows investors to assess recurring earnings power (continuing operations EPS) separately from the one-time effects of disposal (discontinued operations EPS). In this case: Continuing operations EPS = $(500,000) ÷ 1,000,000 = $(0.50); Discontinued operations EPS = $800,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.80.
explanations.c: EPS is still presented when there is a loss from continuing operations — a loss does not eliminate the EPS disclosure requirement. Antidilution provisions affect the exclusion of dilutive securities from the diluted EPS calculation, not the requirement to present EPS itself.
explanations.d: Both continuing operations EPS and discontinued operations EPS must be presented on the face of the income statement — not relegated to footnotes when they are quantitatively significant.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: income statement and statement of profit or loss
questions.text: A company sells its entire consumer electronics division — which constitutes one of its three reportable segments under ASC 280 — as part of a strategic decision to focus on industrial markets. The sale closes on November 30. For the income statement presentation of the current annual period

answers.text: The entire year's results for the consumer electronics division remain in continuing operations since the segment operated normally for most of the year
Only the November 30 gain on disposal is presented as discontinued — the January through November operating results remain in continuing operations
No reclassification is needed — gains on sale of business segments are always presented as extraordinary items under current GAAP

The consumer electronics division's results for the full year (operating income, gain on sale, and related taxes) are presented as a discontinued operation — the disposal of a reportable segment representing a strategic shift qualifies as a discontinued operation

explanations.a: This is incorrect — when a component qualifies as a discontinued operation, all periods presented (including the current full year) are reclassified, not just post-classification periods. The fact that the segment operated normally for most of the year does not prevent reclassification of its full-year results.
explanations.b: Presenting only the gain on disposal as discontinued while leaving 11 months of operating results in continuing operations does not comply with ASC 205-20. All results of the discontinued component for all periods presented are reclassified to discontinued operations.
explanations.c: Extraordinary item classification was eliminated by ASU 2015-01 — there are no extraordinary items under current US GAAP. Gains on business segment disposals are not presented as extraordinary items.
explanations.d: ASC 205-20 specifies that disposal of a reportable segment (a business unit with distinct operations and cash flows) that represents a strategic shift qualifies as a discontinued operation. All of the consumer electronics division's results — operating income from January through November, gain on sale on November 30, and all related income taxes — are reclassified out of continuing operations and presented as discontinued operations for the current year and all comparative periods presented. This allows users to assess what the entity's operations look like without the sold division.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Which of the following items is classified as Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) rather than as a component of net income under US GAAP?

answers.text: Unrealized holding gains and losses on available-for-sale (AFS) debt securities
Realized gains from the sale of equity securities measured at fair value through net income
Dividend income from investments in equity securities
Impairment losses on held-to-maturity debt securities

explanations.a: Under ASC 320-10-45, unrealized holding gains and losses on AFS debt securities are recognized as OCI — they bypass the income statement and accumulate in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) within stockholders' equity until the securities are sold, at which point the gains or losses are reclassified from OCI into net income (a reclassification adjustment).
explanations.b: Realized gains from selling equity securities carried at fair value through net income (FVTNI) are recognized in net income — not OCI. For FVTNI equity securities (which is the default for most equity securities under ASC 321), all changes in fair value (realized and unrealized) flow through net income.
explanations.c: Dividend income from investments in equity securities is recognized in net income regardless of how the securities are classified — dividends do not bypass the income statement.
explanations.d: Impairment losses on held-to-maturity debt securities (when a credit loss exists under the CECL model) are recognized as a credit loss expense in net income — not as OCI. Under ASC 326, expected credit losses on HTM securities reduce the amortized cost basis through a valuation allowance, with the credit loss going through net income.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company holds a portfolio of AFS debt securities. During the year, the fair value of these securities decreased by $80,000 (pre-tax). The income tax rate is 25%. How does this change affect the financial statements?

answers.text: Net income decreases by $60,000; AOCI decreases by $60,000; total stockholders' equity decreases by $60,000
Net income is unaffected; OCI decreases by $60,000 (net of $20,000 tax benefit); AOCI decreases by $60,000; total stockholders' equity decreases by $60,000
Net income is unaffected; OCI decreases by $80,000 (gross, pre-tax); total stockholders' equity decreases by $80,000
Net income decreases by $80,000; total stockholders' equity decreases by $80,000; income tax benefit of $20,000 reduces tax expense in net income

explanations.a: The $60,000 figure (net of tax) is correct, but characterizing this as a decrease in net income is wrong. Unrealized losses on AFS debt securities bypass net income — they are recognized only in OCI, not in net income.
explanations.b: Unrealized holding losses on AFS debt securities are recognized in OCI (bypassing net income) with an associated deferred tax effect. The OCI decrease = $80,000 × (1 - 25%) = $60,000 net of tax. A deferred tax asset of $20,000 is also created ($80,000 × 25%). The net effect on AOCI and total stockholders' equity is a decrease of $60,000. Net income is unaffected.
explanations.c: OCI should be presented net of tax — presenting the gross $80,000 without the tax effect does not comply with ASC 220, which requires OCI items to be presented net of their related tax effects in the statement of comprehensive income.
explanations.d: Unrealized losses on AFS securities do not affect net income — they go directly to OCI. If they affected net income, the income tax benefit would reduce tax expense, but because they bypass net income entirely, the tax effect is recorded as a deferred tax asset with the offset to OCI.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company sells AFS debt securities that had an unrealized gain of $50,000 (net of tax) recognized in AOCI. The sale results in a realized gain of $50,000. How is this transaction reported?

answers.text: Only in OCI — the gain remains in OCI since it was originally recognized there

As a $50,000 realized gain in net income, with a ($50,000) reclassification adjustment removing the amount from OCI — resulting in no net change to comprehensive income but shifting $50,000 from OCI to net income
As a $50,000 gain in net income with no OCI adjustment — the OCI balance for this security simply disappears when the security is sold
As a $100,000 gain in net income ($50,000 previously in OCI plus $50,000 realized at sale) — both amounts are recognized in net income upon sale

explanations.a: Upon sale of AFS securities, previously recognized OCI amounts do not remain in OCI — they are reclassified into net income through a reclassification adjustment. Keeping unrealized gains permanently in OCI even after realization would be incorrect.
explanations.b: ASC 320-10-35-1 requires that when AFS securities are sold, the unrealized gain or loss previously reported in OCI is reclassified into net income as a realized gain or loss (a 'reclassification adjustment'). This process: (1) recognizes the $50,000 realized gain in net income (increasing EPS); and (2) simultaneously records a ($50,000) reclassification adjustment in OCI (removing the previously recognized unrealized gain from AOCI). The net effect on total comprehensive income in the current period is zero for the previously recognized gain — it was already recognized in total comprehensive income when the unrealized gain was first recorded; reclassification just moves it from OCI to net income.
explanations.c: The OCI balance does not simply disappear — it must be formally reclassified through a reclassification adjustment that runs through OCI to prevent double-counting. Without the reclassification adjustment, the same gain would effectively be recognized twice in comprehensive income.
explanations.d: Recognizing $100,000 in net income would result in double-counting — the $50,000 unrealized gain was already included in total comprehensive income when it was recorded in OCI in prior periods. Only the $50,000 realized gain is recognized in net income, and the offsetting reclassification adjustment eliminates it from OCI.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company chooses to present comprehensive income using the 'two-statement approach' rather than the single statement of comprehensive income. Which statement BEST describes the two-statement approach?

answers.text: The entity presents the income statement and balance sheet in one combined statement, with a second statement showing cash flows
The entity presents the statement of cash flows in two sections: operating activities and the combined investing/financing activities

The entity presents a traditional income statement ending with net income, immediately followed by a separate statement of comprehensive income that begins with net income and adds OCI components to arrive at total comprehensive income
The entity presents a condensed income statement for interim periods and a full income statement for the annual period — two levels of income statement detail

explanations.a: The two-statement approach does not combine the income statement and balance sheet. It involves two separate income-related statements — the income statement and the statement of comprehensive income.
explanations.b: The two-statement approach refers to comprehensive income presentation, not to cash flow statement formatting. The cash flow statement has three sections (operating, investing, financing) and is not affected by the comprehensive income presentation choice.
explanations.c: ASC 220-10-45-1 permits two approaches for presenting comprehensive income: (1) the single-statement approach — combining the income statement and statement of OCI into one continuous statement ending with total comprehensive income; or (2) the two-statement approach — a traditional income statement ending with net income, immediately followed by a separate statement of comprehensive income that begins with net income (carried forward from the income statement) and then adds each OCI component to arrive at total comprehensive income. The two statements must be presented together consecutively.
explanations.d: The two-statement approach relates to comprehensive income presentation format — not to the level of detail (condensed vs. full) across reporting periods.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Pension actuarial losses accumulate in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI). Under ASC 715 (using the corridor method), when are these actuarial losses reclassified from AOCI into net income?

answers.text: Immediately in the period they arise — all actuarial losses are recognized in net income when they occur
Never — pension actuarial losses remain permanently in AOCI and are never reclassified to net income
When the pension plan is terminated or when the entity files for bankruptcy

Over future service periods as a component of net periodic pension cost — the excess of AOCI beyond the corridor (10% of the greater of PBO or plan assets) is amortized into net income using the expected average remaining service life of active participants

explanations.a: The immediate recognition approach for pension actuarial gains and losses (recognizing them directly in net income when they occur) is permitted but is not the corridor approach. Under the corridor method, immediate recognition does not occur — instead, amortization over future periods is used.
explanations.b: Actuarial losses in AOCI are not permanent — they are reclassified into net income through the amortization process described in the corridor approach. Some component of accumulated actuarial gains/losses is amortized to net income each period.
explanations.c: Pension plan termination does result in settlement accounting that can reclassify AOCI amounts — but regular actuarial loss amortization does not wait for termination events.
explanations.d: Under the corridor approach (ASC 715-30-55), if the cumulative unrecognized actuarial gain or loss exceeds 10% of the greater of the projected benefit obligation (PBO) or the fair value of plan assets (the 'corridor'), the excess is amortized into net income as a component of net periodic pension cost over the expected average remaining service life of active plan participants. This delayed recognition approach smooths the impact of actuarial volatility on net income.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company designates a pay-fixed, receive-variable interest rate swap as a cash flow hedge of its variable-rate debt. The swap has a fair value gain of $200,000 (pre-tax) and the hedge is highly effective. Where is the effective portion of this gain recognized?

answers.text: Entirely in net income in the current period — all derivative gains and losses are recognized in net income when they arise
In OCI until the hedged cash flows (interest payments) affect earnings — at which point it is reclassified from AOCI into net income as an adjustment to interest expense
In OCI permanently — cash flow hedge gains are never reclassified to net income
Deferred as a liability on the balance sheet until the hedged debt matures

explanations.a: Without hedge accounting designation, derivative gains and losses would flow entirely through net income (mark-to-market). The purpose of cash flow hedge accounting under ASC 815 is specifically to defer the effective portion in OCI to match the timing of recognition with the hedged cash flows — avoiding volatility in net income.
explanations.b: ASC 815-20-35 requires that for a qualifying cash flow hedge, the effective portion of the gain or loss on the hedging instrument (the swap) is recognized in OCI and accumulated in AOCI. The amounts are reclassified from AOCI into net income as a component of interest expense (offsetting the variable interest payments on the hedged debt) in the same period in which the hedged cash flows affect earnings — effectively converting the variable-rate interest expense to an approximately fixed-rate equivalent.
explanations.c: Cash flow hedge OCI amounts are not permanent — they are reclassified into net income when the hedged item affects earnings. This reclassification is the fundamental mechanism of cash flow hedge accounting.
explanations.d: The swap's fair value gain is not deferred as a liability — it is an asset (the swap is in a gain position). The accounting records the fair value of the swap on the balance sheet (as an asset) with the offsetting credit in OCI for the effective portion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: US Company A has a wholly owned subsidiary in France whose functional currency is the Euro. At year-end, Company A translates the subsidiary's financial statements from Euros to US dollars (the reporting currency) using the current rate method. The resulting translation adjustment is

answers.text: Recognized as a gain or loss in net income in the current period — foreign currency translation adjustments are treated like realized foreign exchange gains and losses
Deferred as an asset or liability on Company A's balance sheet until the French subsidiary is sold

Recognized in OCI — the cumulative translation adjustment (CTA) is accumulated in AOCI until the French subsidiary is sold, at which point it is reclassified into net income as part of the gain or loss on disposal
Treated as a change in accounting estimate and recorded prospectively with no cumulative effect

explanations.a: Under ASC 830 (Foreign Currency Matters), translation adjustments arising from translating a foreign subsidiary's functional currency statements into the parent's reporting currency are not recognized in net income. If they were, they would create significant income statement volatility unrelated to the subsidiary's actual operating performance.
explanations.b: The translation adjustment is not deferred as a separate balance sheet asset or liability — it is recognized within stockholders' equity as a component of AOCI (Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income), labeled as the cumulative translation adjustment (CTA).
explanations.c: ASC 830-30-45-12 requires that the aggregate translation adjustment from translating a foreign entity's functional currency financial statements into the reporting currency be recognized in OCI and accumulated in AOCI as the CTA. The CTA remains in AOCI until the entity disposes of the foreign subsidiary — at which point the full CTA related to that subsidiary is released (reclassified) from AOCI into net income as part of the gain or loss on disposal.
explanations.d: Foreign currency translation is a required accounting process under ASC 830 — it is not a change in accounting estimate. The method of translation (current rate method for a foreign functional currency subsidiary) is required by the standard and does not represent an estimate change.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: During the year, a company's AOCI increased by $90,000 (net of tax). Net income was $600,000. Cash dividends declared were $100,000. What is the company's total comprehensive income for the year?

answers.text: $590,000 — net income plus OCI changes, less dividends
$600,000 — comprehensive income equals net income; OCI changes are not included
$700,000 — dividends are added back to net income for comprehensive income purposes
$690,000 — total comprehensive income equals net income plus OCI changes; dividends are not a component of comprehensive income

explanations.a: Dividends are not deducted in calculating comprehensive income. Dividends are a distribution to owners — they are presented in the statement of changes in equity but are not a component of comprehensive income. Deducting dividends would be incorrect.
explanations.b: Comprehensive income includes all changes in equity from non-owner sources — both net income and OCI components. Comprehensive income is therefore broader than net income alone.
explanations.c: Dividends are not added back for comprehensive income purposes. Dividends are owner transactions (distributions) and are excluded from comprehensive income by definition — comprehensive income includes only non-owner changes in equity.
explanations.d: ASC 220-10-20 defines comprehensive income as the change in equity of a business enterprise during a period from transactions and other events and circumstances from non-owner sources — it includes all changes in equity except those resulting from investments by and distributions to owners. Therefore: Total comprehensive income = Net income + OCI = $600,000 + $90,000 = $690,000. Dividends declared ($100,000) are excluded because they represent owner transactions (distributions to shareholders), not income.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: The statement of changes in stockholders' equity presents changes arising from which of the following?

answers.text: Only changes in retained earnings — all other equity components are presented solely on the balance sheet

All transactions and other events that cause changes in the components of stockholders' equity during the period — including net income, OCI, dividends, stock issuances, repurchases, and equity-based compensation
Only external financing activities — equity changes from internal operations are presented on the income statement
Only changes from non-owner sources (net income and OCI) — owner transactions are excluded from the statement

explanations.a: The statement of changes in equity is broader than just retained earnings — it presents changes in all equity components: common stock, APIC, retained earnings, AOCI, and treasury stock.
explanations.b: The statement of changes in stockholders' equity (ASC 505-10-50) reconciles the beginning and ending balances of each equity component by presenting all changes during the period, including: net income (from the income statement); OCI components (from the statement of comprehensive income); dividends declared to shareholders; stock issuances (IPOs, stock options exercised, stock-based compensation vesting); share repurchases (treasury stock); and prior period adjustments. This statement provides a complete linkage between the income statement, OCI, and the equity section of the balance sheet.
explanations.c: The statement of changes in equity includes both owner transactions (financing activities — stock issuances, repurchases, dividends) and non-owner changes (income, OCI). It is not limited to financing activities.
explanations.d: The statement includes both owner transactions (dividends, stock issuances, repurchases) and non-owner changes (net income, OCI). Excluding owner transactions would make it equivalent to the statement of comprehensive income, which is not the purpose of the equity statement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Beginning retained earnings were $420,000. During the year, net income was $180,000, and cash dividends of $55,000 were declared (not yet paid). What is ending retained earnings?

answers.text: $545,000 — beginning RE + net income, excluding unpaid dividends until paid
$600,000 — beginning RE + net income only; dividends reduce cash, not retained earnings
$545,000 — beginning RE ($420,000) + net income ($180,000) - dividends declared ($55,000) = $545,000
$490,000 — beginning RE + net income - dividends paid (assuming dividends were paid during the year)

explanations.a: This response gives the correct answer ($545,000) but provides an incorrect explanation. Dividends reduce retained earnings when declared — not when paid. The question correctly states dividends were declared, so they are deducted in the calculation.
explanations.b: Dividends declared during the period do reduce retained earnings at the date of declaration — not at the date of payment. The journal entry at declaration date is: debit Retained Earnings, credit Dividends Payable. The cash payment subsequently reduces Dividends Payable and cash, with no further effect on retained earnings.
explanations.c: Retained earnings rollforward: Beginning RE + Net income - Dividends declared = $420,000 + $180,000 - $55,000 = $545,000. Dividends reduce retained earnings when declared (regardless of when paid), so the full $55,000 is deducted in the period of declaration.
explanations.d: Ending retained earnings is based on dividends declared — not dividends paid. If dividends were declared but not yet paid, they still reduce retained earnings in the period declared. The $490,000 figure appears to be using an incorrect calculation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company issues 5,000 shares of $2 par value common stock for $18 per share cash. How is this issuance reflected in the statement of changes in stockholders' equity?

answers.text: Common stock increases by $90,000 (5,000 × $18), retained earnings decreases by $90,000 — treasury stock transactions affect retained earnings
Common stock increases by $10,000 (5,000 × $2), retained earnings increases by $80,000 (5,000 × $16 excess)
Common stock increases by $90,000 (5,000 × $18), with no APIC — the full issuance price is recorded in the par value account
Common stock increases by $10,000 (5,000 × $2 par value), additional paid-in capital increases by $80,000 (5,000 × $16 excess over par) — total equity increases by $90,000

explanations.a: Stock issuances affect common stock and APIC — not retained earnings. Retained earnings is affected by net income, dividends, and prior period adjustments — not by stock issuances at prices above par.
explanations.b: The excess over par is recorded in APIC (additional paid-in capital), not in retained earnings. Crediting retained earnings for the excess above par is incorrect.
explanations.c: Recording the full $18 issuance price in the par value (common stock) account is incorrect. The common stock account is credited for par value only ($2 × 5,000 = $10,000); the excess above par ($16 × 5,000 = $80,000) is credited to additional paid-in capital.
explanations.d: Stock issuances are recorded by crediting common stock at par value and crediting APIC for the excess above par: Common stock = 5,000 × $2 = $10,000; APIC = 5,000 × ($18 - $2) = $80,000. Total proceeds of $90,000 = $10,000 (common stock) + $80,000 (APIC). Both common stock and APIC increase, and total stockholders' equity increases by $90,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company repurchases 3,000 shares of its $1 par common stock at $30 per share and records the transaction using the cost method. What is the effect on the statement of changes in stockholders' equity?

answers.text: Treasury stock increases by $90,000 (3,000 × $30), reducing total stockholders' equity by $90,000 — common stock and APIC are unchanged
Common stock decreases by $3,000 and retained earnings decreases by $87,000 — reflecting the cost method
Retained earnings decreases by $90,000 — share repurchases always reduce retained earnings under US GAAP
Treasury stock increases by $3,000 (par value) and APIC decreases by $87,000 — the excess above par reduces APIC

explanations.a: Under the cost method (ASC 505-30), treasury stock repurchases are recorded at the full cost of repurchase in the treasury stock contra-equity account — no separate entries to common stock or APIC at the time of repurchase. Treasury stock increases by $90,000 (3,000 × $30), reducing total stockholders' equity by $90,000. The common stock and APIC accounts are not affected at repurchase under the cost method.
explanations.b: The cost method does not reduce common stock and retained earnings at repurchase — that characterization describes the retirement method (when shares are formally retired). Under the cost method, the full repurchase cost goes to treasury stock.
explanations.c: Retained earnings is not directly debited in a treasury stock repurchase under the cost method. Retained earnings is only affected when treasury shares are retired (if cost exceeds APIC available) or when treasury shares are reissued below cost (excess charge to retained earnings).
explanations.d: The par value method is a different accounting approach from the cost method. Under the par value method, common stock is debited at par and APIC is debited for the original issuance excess — but the question specifies the cost method, which records the full cost in a single treasury stock account.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company has 200,000 shares outstanding with a market price of $30 per share and a par value of $1 per share. The board declares a 10% stock dividend. Which journal entry correctly records the stock dividend?

answers.text: Debit retained earnings $200,000 (20,000 new shares × $1 par); credit common stock $200,000
Debit retained earnings $600,000 (20,000 × $30 market price); credit common stock $20,000 (20,000 × $1 par); credit additional paid-in capital $580,000 (20,000 × $29)
No journal entry is required — stock dividends do not affect equity balances, only the number of shares
Debit retained earnings $600,000; credit paid-in capital from stock dividends $600,000 — APIC is not credited for stock dividends

explanations.a: For a small stock dividend (less than 20-25% of outstanding shares — this 10% qualifies), the stock dividend is recorded at fair market value, not par value. Recording only at par value understates the charge to retained earnings.
explanations.b: A small stock dividend (under 20-25%) is recorded at the current market price of the shares issued. For the 20,000 new shares (200,000 × 10%): Debit Retained Earnings = 20,000 × $30 = $600,000; Credit Common Stock = 20,000 × $1 par = $20,000; Credit Additional Paid-in Capital = 20,000 × ($30 - $1) = $580,000. This reflects that shareholders receive shares with a fair value equal to the market price, and retained earnings is reduced by the equivalent value transferred to the capital accounts.
explanations.c: Stock dividends do affect equity balances — retained earnings decreases and contributed capital (common stock + APIC) increases by an equal amount. The total stockholders' equity remains the same (it is a reclassification within equity), but the individual components change.
explanations.d: APIC (additional paid-in capital) is credited for the excess above par in a small stock dividend. The description 'paid-in capital from stock dividends' is a valid label for what is essentially an APIC credit — but debiting retained earnings and crediting a generic paid-in capital account for the full $600,000 (without separately crediting common stock for par value) would be incorrect.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: The board of directors appropriates $400,000 of retained earnings for a future factory expansion. How does this appropriation affect the statement of changes in equity and total stockholders' equity?

answers.text: Total stockholders' equity decreases by $400,000 — retained earnings is reduced by the appropriation

Total stockholders' equity is unchanged — the appropriation reclassifies $400,000 from unappropriated retained earnings to appropriated retained earnings within the same equity section, with no net effect on total equity
Total stockholders' equity increases by $400,000 — appropriating retained earnings signals financial strength and market confidence
The appropriation creates a liability to the factory expansion project — it is removed from stockholders' equity and recognized as a deferred capital obligation

explanations.a: An appropriation of retained earnings does not reduce total stockholders' equity — it merely reclassifies amounts between retained earnings sub-categories. No economic resources leave the entity; no asset is affected.
explanations.b: A board appropriation of retained earnings is a journal entry that debits unappropriated retained earnings and credits appropriated retained earnings (a sub-account of retained earnings). Both accounts are within stockholders' equity, so total equity is unchanged. The appropriation communicates to financial statement users that a portion of retained earnings has been designated for a specific purpose and is not available for dividends — it is a disclosure tool, not an accounting event that affects total equity.
explanations.c: An appropriation does not increase total equity — it is an internal reclassification within equity. Total equity is determined by net assets, not by how retained earnings sub-accounts are labeled.
explanations.d: An appropriation of retained earnings does not create a liability. No obligation to a third party is created — retained earnings remains within stockholders' equity. The appropriation simply designates that $400,000 of retained earnings is earmarked for a future purpose.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: During the year, the following equity changes occurred: stock issuance for $250,000; net income of $350,000; dividends declared of $90,000; and OCI loss of $40,000. Beginning stockholders' equity was $2,000,000. What is ending stockholders' equity?

answers.text: $2,430,000 — beginning equity + stock issuance + net income; dividends and OCI excluded
$2,470,000 — beginning equity + all increases, ignoring decreases
$2,560,000 — beginning equity + stock issuance + net income + OCI; dividends excluded since they reduce only cash
$2,470,000 — beginning equity ($2,000,000) + stock issuance ($250,000) + net income ($350,000) - dividends declared ($90,000) - OCI loss ($40,000) = $2,470,000

explanations.a: $2,430,000 omits both dividends and OCI. Both must be included: dividends reduce retained earnings when declared; OCI changes affect AOCI, both of which are components of total stockholders' equity.
explanations.b: $2,470,000 is the correct answer, but reached here by incorrectly ignoring decreases — both dividends and OCI loss are decreases that must be reflected.
explanations.c: $2,560,000 incorrectly excludes dividends. Dividends declared reduce retained earnings — they reduce equity even though no cash has left the entity yet (a dividends payable liability is created).
explanations.d: Total stockholders' equity is the sum of all equity components. Changes come from: stock issuance (+$250,000), net income (+$350,000), dividends declared (-$90,000), and OCI loss (-$40,000). Beginning equity ($2,000,000) + $250,000 + $350,000 - $90,000 - $40,000 = $2,470,000. This correctly includes all owner and non-owner changes in equity for the period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: During the current year's audit, the company discovers that net income in Year 2 was overstated by $300,000 due to incorrect capitalization of expenses (the overstatement is material). The current year is Year 4, and the company presents Year 3 and Year 4 comparative financial statements. Under ASC 250, how is this error corrected in the statement of changes in equity?

answers.text: The $300,000 correction is recorded in Year 4 net income — errors discovered in the current year are corrected through current-year income
The $300,000 correction is disclosed in the footnotes only — retrospective restatement is optional for non-recurring errors

The beginning retained earnings of Year 3 (the earliest period presented) is adjusted downward by the after-tax amount of the error, with all prior periods presented restated to correct the error, and comparative statements reflecting the corrected amounts
The error correction is recorded as an extraordinary item in Year 4 to clearly separate it from normal operations

explanations.a: Under ASC 250-10-45, material errors from prior periods are not corrected through current-year income — they require retrospective restatement of prior periods. Correcting through current-year income would misstate current operating results.
explanations.b: Retrospective restatement is not optional for material errors — ASC 250-10-45-23 requires retrospective correction of material prior-period errors by restatement. Footnote-only disclosure is insufficient when the error is material.
explanations.c: ASC 250-10-45-23 requires that a material prior period error be corrected by retroactively restating prior period financial statements. When Year 2 (before the comparative period begins) contained the error, the correction appears as an adjustment to beginning retained earnings of the earliest period presented (Year 3). The Year 3 statement of changes in equity shows beginning retained earnings restated to reflect the Year 2 error correction, with appropriate footnote disclosure explaining the restatement. If Year 2 were presented comparatively, it would be restated directly.
explanations.d: Extraordinary item classification was eliminated by ASU 2015-01. Prior period error corrections are not extraordinary items under current US GAAP — they are reported as prior period adjustments through beginning retained earnings.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: The statement of cash flows is organized into which three sections?

answers.text: Revenue activities, expense activities, and financing activities
Current activities, non-current activities, and equity activities
Operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities
Cash receipts, cash payments, and non-cash disclosures

explanations.a: Revenue and expense activities describe the income statement — not the structure of the cash flow statement. The cash flow statement focuses on cash inflows and outflows, not on revenue and expense recognition.
explanations.b: Current and non-current is a balance sheet classification framework — not the cash flow statement's structure. The cash flow statement does not mirror the balance sheet's liquidity-based classification.
explanations.c: ASC 230-10-45 requires the statement of cash flows to be divided into three sections: (1) operating activities — cash flows from the entity's primary revenue-generating activities and other transactions not classified as investing or financing; (2) investing activities — cash flows from acquiring and disposing of long-term assets and investments; and (3) financing activities — cash flows from transactions with the entity's owners and creditors related to equity issuances, debt borrowings, and their repayments.
explanations.d: While 'cash receipts and payments' describes the direct method of presenting operating activities, it is not the three-section classification structure of the statement. Non-cash disclosures are supplemental — they are not one of the three sections.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company pays $2.5 million cash to purchase new manufacturing equipment. How is this payment classified on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: As a cash outflow from investing activities — capital expenditures for long-lived assets used in operations are investing activities
As a cash outflow from operating activities — manufacturing equipment is used to produce inventory, which is an operating purpose
As a cash outflow from financing activities — capital expenditures are funded by debt and equity financing
As a non-cash activity disclosed supplementally — equipment purchases are never reflected in the cash flow body

explanations.a: ASC 230-10-45-12 classifies cash payments to acquire property, plant, and equipment as investing activities. Investing activities include: (1) acquiring and disposing of long-lived productive assets; (2) acquiring and disposing of investment securities; and (3) making and collecting loans. The purchase of manufacturing equipment — a long-lived productive asset — is a capital expenditure classified as an investing outflow, regardless of the equipment's operating purpose.
explanations.b: Equipment purchases are not operating activities. The operational purpose of the equipment (manufacturing inventory) does not determine the cash flow classification — the nature of the asset (long-lived productive asset) determines the classification as investing.
explanations.c: Financing activities relate to changes in the entity's equity and debt structure — borrowing, repaying debt, and equity transactions. Spending cash to acquire equipment is an investing activity, not a financing activity.
explanations.d: Only transactions with no cash component are disclosed as non-cash activities. Paying $2.5 million cash for equipment involves a direct cash payment and is presented in the body of the cash flow statement as an investing outflow.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company borrows $3 million under a new long-term bank loan. How is this cash receipt classified on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: As a cash inflow from operating activities — borrowing is needed to fund ongoing operations
As a non-cash supplemental disclosure — debt transactions do not involve cash
As a cash inflow from investing activities — debt is used to fund capital investments
As a cash inflow from financing activities — proceeds from borrowing are a financing activity

explanations.a: Financing activities — not operating activities — include transactions with creditors and owners related to the entity's capital structure. Operating activities reflect the primary business operations and working capital changes.
explanations.b: Borrowing $3 million involves receipt of actual cash. Only transactions with no cash component (e.g., acquiring equipment by issuing a note directly to the seller) are disclosed as non-cash supplemental activities.
explanations.c: Investing activities cover the acquisition and disposal of long-lived assets and investment securities. Borrowing cash is a transaction with a creditor affecting the entity's capital structure — it is financing, not investing.
explanations.d: ASC 230-10-45-14 classifies proceeds from borrowing — including short-term and long-term debt — as cash inflows from financing activities. Financing activities include: (1) borrowing from creditors and repaying debt principal; (2) issuing and repurchasing equity; and (3) paying dividends to shareholders. Receiving $3 million from a bank loan is a financing inflow.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under the indirect method, depreciation expense is added back to net income in the operating activities section because

answers.text: Depreciation reduced net income but required no cash outflow — adding it back adjusts net income to reflect the cash actually generated from operations
Depreciation is a cash expense that must be separately disclosed from other operating cash flows
Depreciation is an investing activity, so it must be moved from operating to investing in the reconciliation
Adding depreciation back increases reported cash from operations, which improves the entity's apparent liquidity for lenders

explanations.a: The indirect method reconciles net income to cash from operations by adding back non-cash expenses (like depreciation) and deducting non-cash revenues, then adjusting for working capital changes. Depreciation reduces net income under accrual accounting, but because no cash leaves the entity, net income understates cash generated from operations by the amount of depreciation. Adding depreciation back restores the cash that was never actually used — it effectively 'undoes' the non-cash expense deduction.
explanations.b: Depreciation is a non-cash expense — it does not involve any cash. It is added back precisely because it is not a cash outflow; it reduced net income without reducing cash.
explanations.c: Depreciation is not moved to investing activities. The investing section reflects actual cash paid for capital assets; depreciation (an allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life) stays in the operating section reconciliation as an add-back.
explanations.d: While adding back depreciation mathematically increases operating cash flow in the indirect method presentation, this is the correct accounting treatment — not a manipulation for appearance purposes. The add-back simply reverses the effect of a non-cash charge.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company acquires equipment worth $600,000 by issuing a note payable directly to the equipment seller — no cash changes hands. How is this transaction presented on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: As a $600,000 investing outflow and a $600,000 financing inflow — because both investing and financing would have occurred if cash were used
As a $600,000 investing outflow only — the note payable is not reflected since the seller financed the transaction
As a supplemental schedule of non-cash investing and financing activities — the transaction is disclosed separately but not presented in the body of the cash flow statement
Not disclosed at all — the transaction is an operating matter between two parties and does not affect the cash flow statement

explanations.a: This 'gross-up' approach would misrepresent the entity's cash position — no cash actually moved. Presenting it as both an inflow and outflow would inflate both sections of the cash flow statement and overstate the entity's investing and financing activity.
explanations.b: Presenting only one side of a non-cash transaction in the body would also misrepresent cash activity. Since no cash flowed, nothing appears in the body of the cash flow statement.
explanations.c: ASC 230-10-50-3 requires significant non-cash investing and financing activities to be disclosed, either in a supplemental schedule accompanying the cash flow statement or in the notes. The equipment acquisition for a note payable is a non-cash investing activity (asset acquired) and non-cash financing activity (obligation incurred) — both sides are disclosed in the supplemental non-cash section. This provides users information about the transaction's economic substance without falsely implying cash flows occurred.
explanations.d: Non-cash investing and financing activities must be disclosed — they are not omitted. While they don't appear in the body of the statement, ASC 230 requires supplemental disclosure of significant non-cash transactions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under US GAAP (ASC 230), how is interest paid by a non-financial entity classified on the statement of cash flows, and how does this differ from IFRS?

answers.text: Under US GAAP, interest paid is classified as an operating activity — no options are permitted; under IFRS, interest paid may be classified as operating or financing (entity's accounting policy choice)
Under both US GAAP and IFRS, interest paid is classified as a financing activity — it relates to the cost of borrowing
Under US GAAP, interest paid is classified as an investing activity; under IFRS, it must be classified as operating
Under both standards, interest paid may be classified as either operating or financing — the choice is the same under both

explanations.a: ASC 230-10-45-17 classifies interest paid (and interest and dividends received) as operating activities for non-financial entities under US GAAP — this is a requirement with no alternative.
