IFRS (IAS 7.31-33) allows entities to classify interest paid as either operating activities (to be consistent with interest expense in profit or loss) or financing activities (as a cost of obtaining financial resources). This flexibility under IFRS represents a significant difference from US GAAP's mandatory operating classification.
explanations.b: Under US GAAP, interest paid is operating — not financing. Under IFRS, entities may choose financing as one option, but it is not universal.
explanations.c: Under US GAAP, interest paid is operating — not investing. Under IFRS, interest paid can be operating or financing, but not investing.
explanations.d: US GAAP does not offer the option to classify interest paid as financing — it is mandatory operating for non-financial entities. IFRS offers flexibility; US GAAP does not.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company uses the indirect method. During the year, accounts receivable increased from $300,000 to $450,000. Net income was $800,000. How does the $150,000 increase in accounts receivable affect the operating activities section?

answers.text: Added to net income — an increase in AR means more cash was collected than revenue recognized
No effect — AR changes are balance sheet items and do not affect the operating section
Added to net income — because AR represents future cash inflows
Subtracted from net income — the AR increase means revenue was recognized on credit without cash receipt, so reported net income overstates cash collected from customers

explanations.a: The relationship is reversed. An increase in AR means cash collections LAGGED behind recognized revenue — more revenue was booked than cash received. This requires a subtraction, not an addition.
explanations.b: Working capital changes (current assets and liabilities) are specifically included in the operating activities section under the indirect method. The indirect method reconciles net income to cash by adjusting for non-cash items (depreciation, amortization) and working capital changes (AR, inventory, AP, etc.).
explanations.c: AR does represent future cash inflows, but that future component has already been included in net income via revenue recognition. The indirect method adjustment removes this non-cash portion of net income.
explanations.d: An increase in accounts receivable of $150,000 means the company recognized $150,000 more in revenue than it actually collected in cash. Under the indirect method, this excess non-cash revenue must be subtracted from net income to arrive at cash generated from operations. Operating cash from sales = Net sales recognized - Increase in AR = Net income starting point is adjusted by subtracting the $150,000 AR increase. Conversely, a decrease in AR would be added back (collected more cash than revenue recognized).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company repurchases 5,000 of its own shares (treasury stock) at $20 per share for $100,000. The same year, it purchases 10,000 shares of another publicly traded company's stock as a long-term equity investment for $200,000. How are these two transactions classified on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: Both are investing activities — both involve purchasing stock
Both are financing activities — both involve equity transactions
Treasury stock repurchase: financing activity; purchase of another company's stock: investing activity — the nature of the entity relationship determines the classification
Treasury stock repurchase: operating activity; purchase of another company's stock: investing activity

explanations.a: Both involve purchasing stock, but the nature of the stock determines classification. Repurchasing a company's own stock reduces equity (a capital structure transaction = financing); purchasing another company's stock acquires an investment asset (= investing).
explanations.b: Purchasing another company's stock is an investing activity — it acquires an investment asset, not a capital structure transaction.
explanations.c: ASC 230-10-45-15 classifies treasury stock repurchases as financing activities — they represent a return of equity capital to shareholders, affecting the entity's capital structure. ASC 230-10-45-12 classifies purchases of equity securities of other companies (investments) as investing activities — they represent acquisition of investment assets. The key distinction is whether the entity is transacting with its own equity structure (financing) or acquiring assets of other entities (investing).
explanations.d: Treasury stock repurchases are financing activities — not operating activities. Operating activities reflect the primary business operations and working capital management.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: When is a company required to consolidate a subsidiary under US GAAP?

answers.text: When the investor has a controlling financial interest in the subsidiary — generally achieved through ownership of more than 50% of the subsidiary's voting stock, or by being the primary beneficiary of a variable interest entity (VIE)
When the investor owns exactly 50% of the subsidiary — equal ownership requires consolidated presentation
When the investor owns more than 20% but less than 50% — this range always requires consolidation
Consolidation is optional — entities may choose between consolidation and the equity method for any majority-owned subsidiary

explanations.a: ASC 810-10 requires consolidation when a reporting entity has a controlling financial interest in another entity. The most common indicator of control is ownership of more than 50% of the voting stock — which gives the parent the ability to direct the activities of the subsidiary. Additionally, entities that are VIEs must be consolidated by their primary beneficiary — the entity that has power over significant activities and absorbs a majority of expected losses or residual returns.
explanations.b: Exactly 50% ownership does not constitute control — decisions would require mutual agreement of both 50% owners. Control requires the ability to direct activities unilaterally.
explanations.c: Ownership of 20%-50% of voting stock generally indicates significant influence — leading to equity method accounting, not consolidation. Consolidation requires more than 50% ownership or control through VIE status or other controlling interests.
explanations.d: Consolidation is not optional when a controlling financial interest exists. ASC 810 requires consolidation of controlled entities — management cannot simply choose the equity method for a majority-owned subsidiary.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Parent Company owns 80% of Subsidiary. The remaining 20% is owned by unrelated outside investors. On the consolidated balance sheet, the 20% interest held by outside investors is presented as

answers.text: A liability — the parent has a constructive obligation to the minority owners
As a deduction from consolidated assets — minority interest reduces the entity's net assets
As a separate component of consolidated stockholders' equity, labeled 'Non-controlling interest' — presented within total equity but separately from the parent's equity
Not presented — only assets and liabilities attributable to the 80% parent interest are included in consolidation

explanations.a: Non-controlling interest is not a liability — the outside investors have an equity interest, not a creditor claim. ASC 810-10-45-16 explicitly requires NCI to be classified as equity.
explanations.b: NCI is not a deduction from assets. It is presented within stockholders' equity — the consolidated balance sheet includes 100% of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities, and NCI is the portion of equity attributable to the non-controlling shareholders.
explanations.c: ASC 810-10-45-16 requires that non-controlling interest (NCI) be presented within consolidated stockholders' equity, separately from the parent's equity. The consolidated statements include 100% of the subsidiary's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses — the NCI represents the minority shareholders' proportionate ownership of the subsidiary's net assets, presented as a distinct component of consolidated equity.
explanations.d: All of the subsidiary's assets and liabilities are included in consolidation (100%), not just the 80% owned by the parent. The NCI represents the outside owners' stake in those fully consolidated assets and liabilities.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Parent owns 90% of Subsidiary. During the year, Subsidiary sold $500,000 of inventory to Parent at a 30% gross margin (cost = $350,000). At year-end, Parent still holds $200,000 of this inventory in its warehouse (at transfer price). Which consolidation elimination is required?

answers.text: Eliminate $500,000 of intercompany sales revenue and $350,000 of cost of goods sold — no inventory adjustment is required since the goods have been paid for
Eliminate the full $200,000 of ending inventory — intercompany goods remaining in inventory are entirely removed from consolidated statements
No elimination is needed for goods not yet sold to outside parties — intercompany profits are only eliminated when the goods are ultimately sold outside the consolidated group
Eliminate $60,000 of unrealized intercompany profit in ending inventory — debit cost of goods sold $60,000 and credit inventory $60,000, in addition to eliminating the intercompany sale

explanations.a: Eliminating only the sales and cost in a period without adjusting ending inventory would leave an unrealized profit in the inventory balance. The intercompany sale has already been eliminated in the income statement, but $60,000 of gross profit remains embedded in the ending inventory value on Parent's books.
explanations.b: Eliminating the full $200,000 of inventory would remove both the cost and the profit, understating the consolidated inventory. Only the unrealized profit portion ($60,000) is eliminated — the cost component ($140,000) represents a real economic cost to the consolidated entity.
explanations.c: Elimination of intercompany profits is required for goods still within the consolidated group at year-end — it is not deferred until the goods are sold externally. If not eliminated, the consolidated balance sheet would overstate inventory and the income statement would overstate consolidated profit.
explanations.d: The unrealized intercompany profit in ending inventory must be eliminated. Subsidiary sold $500,000 at a 30% margin — the markup per dollar of transfer price is approximately $150,000 on $500,000 of sales. Of the $200,000 remaining in Parent's inventory, the embedded profit = $200,000 × 30% / (1 + 30%) ≈ $46,154 — actually the simpler calculation: Gross margin % based on cost = $150,000/$350,000. Simpler approach: If GM% = 30% of selling price, then on $200,000 remaining, the unrealized profit = $200,000 × 30% = $60,000. The consolidation entry eliminates this $60,000 by debiting COGS (reducing consolidated income) and crediting inventory (reducing the inflated inventory balance). In subsequent periods when the goods are sold externally, the profit will be recognized.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASC 805 (Business Combinations), Company A acquires 100% of Company B for $10 million cash. The fair value of Company B's identifiable net assets at acquisition is $8 million. How is goodwill recognized and subsequently measured?

answers.text: Goodwill of $2 million is recognized; it is amortized over 40 years under current US GAAP
No goodwill is recognized — the $2 million excess is charged immediately to expense as a transaction cost
Goodwill of $2 million is expensed immediately in the income statement — paying above fair value is considered an economic loss
Goodwill of $2 million is recognized as an intangible asset — it is tested for impairment annually (at the reporting unit level) and is not amortized by public entities under US GAAP

explanations.a: Goodwill is no longer amortized under US GAAP for public companies. ASC 350-20 eliminated goodwill amortization for public entities in 2001 (SFAS 142). Private companies may elect the private company alternative to amortize goodwill over up to 10 years under ASU 2014-02.
explanations.b: The $2 million excess of acquisition price over identifiable net assets is recognized as goodwill — not expensed as a transaction cost. Transaction costs (advisory fees, legal fees) are expensed separately.
explanations.c: Goodwill is not immediately expensed — it is recognized as an intangible asset representing the future economic benefits arising from synergies, assembled workforce, and other factors that cannot be individually identified and separately recognized.
explanations.d: ASC 805-30-30 defines goodwill as the excess of consideration transferred over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired. The $2 million goodwill is recognized as an intangible asset on the consolidated balance sheet. Under ASC 350-20, goodwill is not amortized by public companies but is tested for impairment at least annually at the reporting unit level (or more frequently if triggering events occur). An impairment exists when the carrying amount of the reporting unit exceeds its fair value.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Which entity must consolidate a variable interest entity (VIE) under ASC 810?

answers.text: The primary beneficiary — the variable interest holder that has both (1) the power to direct the VIE's most significant activities and (2) the obligation to absorb significant losses or the right to receive significant benefits
The entity that owns the largest equity investment in the VIE — the largest investor always consolidates
All entities that have any variable interest in the VIE must consolidate proportionately
No entity consolidates a VIE — VIEs are kept off-balance-sheet and disclosed only in footnotes

explanations.a: ASC 810-10-25 establishes that the primary beneficiary of a VIE must consolidate it. The primary beneficiary is identified as the entity that has: (1) the power to direct the activities of the VIE that most significantly impact its economic performance — for example, the ability to direct operations, make key decisions about assets; AND (2) an obligation to absorb losses or a right to receive benefits that could potentially be significant to the VIE. Both criteria must be met by the same entity for consolidation to be required.
explanations.b: The largest equity investor is not automatically the primary beneficiary. A VIE is specifically characterized by insufficient equity at risk — voting control may not be proportional to economic risk absorption. The entity directing significant activities AND absorbing significant risk is the primary beneficiary.
explanations.c: Proportionate consolidation is generally not permitted under US GAAP for VIEs or subsidiaries. Only the primary beneficiary consolidates the VIE.
explanations.d: VIEs were brought onto balance sheets specifically to address off-balance-sheet financing abuses. ASC 810 requires the primary beneficiary to consolidate the VIE fully — it is not left off-balance-sheet.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Parent (80% owner) sells inventory to Subsidiary at a 25% markup over cost. Subsidiary holds all of this inventory at year-end. The downstream intercompany sale profit must be eliminated. What portion of the unrealized profit is eliminated against the non-controlling interest (NCI)?

answers.text: 20% of the unrealized profit is eliminated against NCI — the NCI bears its proportionate share of the downstream elimination
None — downstream intercompany profits (parent to subsidiary) are fully eliminated against the controlling interest's retained earnings; NCI is not affected by downstream eliminations
50% is eliminated against NCI — intercompany eliminations are always split evenly between controlling and non-controlling interests
100% of the unrealized profit is charged to NCI — the NCI bears all intercompany risks

explanations.a: In a downstream sale (parent selling to subsidiary), the profit originates from the parent — 100% of the unrealized profit belongs to the parent's ownership. There is no rationale for allocating a portion of a downstream elimination to NCI.
explanations.b: For downstream intercompany transactions (parent → subsidiary), the unrealized profit was generated by the parent and resides entirely in the parent's investment in the subsidiary. The full unrealized profit is eliminated against the controlling interest's (parent's) retained earnings — the NCI's share of consolidated equity is not reduced by this elimination. This contrasts with upstream transactions (subsidiary → parent), where the unrealized profit may be allocated proportionately between controlling and non-controlling interests.
explanations.c: Downstream eliminations are not split evenly. The 50/50 split has no basis in ASC 810 — elimination methodology depends on whether the transaction is upstream or downstream.
explanations.d: Charging 100% of the downstream elimination to NCI would incorrectly burden the non-controlling shareholders with a profit they did not generate. The downstream profit was generated by the parent entity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: In a business combination under ASC 805, the acquisition agreement includes contingent consideration: the acquirer will pay an additional $5 million if the acquired entity meets earnings targets over the next two years. At the acquisition date, this contingent consideration has an estimated fair value of $2 million (classified as a liability). One year later, the fair value increases to $3 million due to favorable operating results. How is the $1 million change recognized?

answers.text: As a $1 million addition to goodwill — adjustments to contingent consideration always affect goodwill

As a $1 million loss recognized in earnings in the current period — subsequent changes in the fair value of contingent consideration classified as a liability are recognized in income, not as adjustments to goodwill
As a credit to APIC — changes in contingent consideration are equity transactions
Deferred until the two-year measurement period ends — no recognition until the contingency resolves

explanations.a: Under ASC 805-30-35, goodwill is not subsequently adjusted for changes in the fair value of contingent consideration. The measurement period for adjustments to the acquisition date fair value is limited to one year after acquisition, and those adjustments must relate to new information about facts and circumstances that existed at acquisition — not subsequent changes in operating performance.
explanations.b: ASC 805-30-35-1 distinguishes between measurement period adjustments (which may affect goodwill) and subsequent changes in fair value (which do not affect goodwill). Once past the measurement period, changes in the fair value of contingent consideration classified as a financial liability under ASC 480 or 815 are recognized in earnings. The $1 million increase in fair value of the contingent liability is a loss in the income statement — reflecting that the likelihood of paying additional consideration has increased.
explanations.c: Contingent consideration classified as a liability is not an equity transaction. Changes in liability fair values flow through the income statement (for financial liabilities), not through equity.
explanations.d: Deferring recognition would not comply with ASC 805 or the general principle of recognizing financial liabilities at fair value each reporting period. Changes in fair value are recognized immediately in earnings.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Investor owns 30% of Investee's common stock and has significant influence but not control over Investee's operations. Investee reports net income of $500,000 and declares dividends of $100,000 during the year. Under the equity method, what does Investor recognize?

answers.text: Dividend income of $30,000 — only dividends received are recognized under the equity method
Investment income of $150,000 and a deduction of $30,000 for dividends received — dividends are deducted from investment income
Investment income of $150,000; dividends of $30,000 received reduce the carrying value of the investment — the investment account increases by $120,000 net
No income — the equity method requires waiting until Investee's financial statements are finalized before recognition

explanations.a: Under the equity method, the investor does not recognize dividend income for dividends from the investee — dividends represent a return of investment, reducing the carrying amount of the investment. Recognizing dividends as income would constitute double-counting (since the investor already recognizes its share of the investee's net income).
explanations.b: Dividends are not deducted from investment income in the equity method — they reduce the carrying value of the investment directly. Investment income equals only the investor's share of the investee's net income.
explanations.c: ASC 323-10-35 describes equity method accounting: (1) the investor recognizes its proportionate share of the investee's net income as equity method income — $500,000 × 30% = $150,000, increasing the investment's carrying value; (2) dividends received from the investee are treated as a return of capital, reducing the investment's carrying value — $100,000 × 30% = $30,000. Net change in the investment: +$150,000 - $30,000 = +$120,000. This prevents double-counting since dividends merely distribute previously recognized earnings.
explanations.d: The equity method requires current-period recognition of the investee's results — not deferral until finalization. The investor recognizes its share of the investee's income in the same period the investee earns it, adjusting for any reporting lag.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: The first note to the financial statements typically contains

answers.text: The auditor's explanation of the audit approach and key procedures performed
A summary of significant accounting policies — including the basis of presentation, consolidation principles, revenue recognition method, inventory costing method, and depreciation methods used
Management's discussion and analysis of operations and financial results
A reconciliation of net income to cash flows from operating activities

explanations.a: The audit approach and key procedures are documented in the auditor's workpapers — not in the financial statement notes. The first note does not describe the audit.
explanations.b: ASC 235-10-50 requires disclosure of significant accounting policies — generally presented as the first note to the financial statements. This note describes the critical accounting choices and methods that affect how the financial statements are prepared, including: the basis of consolidation (what entities are included), revenue recognition policies, inventory measurement basis (FIFO, LIFO, weighted average), depreciation methods and useful lives, and other significant policies. This note is essential context for users to understand and interpret all other financial statement amounts.
explanations.c: Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) is presented in annual reports by SEC registrants — but it is a separate section from the financial statement notes and is not the first note. MD&A is unaudited management commentary.
explanations.d: The reconciliation of net income to cash from operations appears in the statement of cash flows itself (under the indirect method) — not in the first note to the financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASC 825-10-50, a company must disclose concentrations of credit risk when

answers.text: Any single customer represents more than 5% of total revenue — a fixed threshold applies
Management decides the concentration is noteworthy — disclosure is entirely at management's discretion
The SEC specifically requests disclosure of customer concentrations in the entity's industry

The entity has significant concentrations of credit risk arising from financial instruments — for example, if a single counterparty, region, or industry accounts for a substantial portion of the entity's receivables, creating significant risk if that counterparty encounters financial difficulty

explanations.a: No specific percentage threshold triggers concentration disclosure under ASC 825 — the standard requires disclosure of significant concentrations that create material risk, determined by judgment rather than a fixed percentage.
explanations.b: Concentration disclosure is not entirely discretionary — ASC 825-10-50-21 requires disclosure when a concentration creates a significant risk of loss. Management must evaluate concentrations objectively and disclose those that are significant.
explanations.c: The SEC may have specific disclosure requirements for its registrants, but the GAAP requirement applies broadly — not only when the SEC requests it.
explanations.d: ASC 825-10-50-20 through 50-22 requires entities to disclose information about significant concentrations of credit risk for all financial instruments. Concentrations to disclose include: significant exposure to a single counterparty, a group of counterparties in the same industry or geographic region, or financial instruments of the same type. The disclosure should describe the activity, region, or economic characteristic that identifies the concentration, and the maximum amount of loss that would be incurred if all parties to the financial instruments failed to perform completely.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASC 850, which information about related party transactions is required to be disclosed in the notes?

answers.text: The nature of the relationship, a description of the transaction, the dollar amounts involved, and amounts due to or from related parties — even if the transactions are at arm's-length terms
Only related party transactions that resulted in material gains or losses to the entity — immaterial transactions need not be disclosed
Only transactions where the related party controls the entity — transactions with entities under common control are not required disclosures
The total amount of all transactions with all affiliates combined — individual transaction details are not required

explanations.a: ASC 850-10-50 requires disclosure of material related party transactions including: (1) the nature of the relationship (e.g., parent-subsidiary, common ownership, officer relationship); (2) a description of the transactions; (3) the dollar amounts of the transactions; (4) amounts due to or from related parties and terms and manner of settlement; and (5) if the entity claims the transactions were at arm's-length terms, the representation must be supportable. This disclosure applies regardless of whether transactions are at market terms — the relationship itself creates relevance for financial statement users.
explanations.b: Materiality applies to required disclosures generally, but the disclosure threshold for related party transactions requires judgment — transactions that might appear numerically small could be qualitatively significant due to the relationship. ASC 850 does not exempt immaterial transactions categorically.
explanations.c: Common control transactions are specifically within the scope of related party disclosure. Transactions with entities under common control (such as sibling subsidiaries of the same parent) require disclosure — often even more so than arm's-length transactions.
explanations.d: Individual transaction details are required — not just an aggregate total. Users need to understand the nature, amount, and terms of significant individual related party transactions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A manufacturing company has a non-cancellable purchase commitment to buy 100,000 units of raw material at $10 per unit over the next 3 years. Current market price is $8 per unit. Under US GAAP, how is this commitment addressed in the financial statements?

answers.text: No disclosure needed until the goods are actually purchased — future commitments are off-balance-sheet and not disclosed
The entire $1 million (100,000 × $10) commitment is recognized as a liability on the balance sheet
A loss accrual of $200,000 [(100,000 × ($10 - $8)] is recognized in the income statement, and the nature of the commitment is disclosed in the notes — the executory contract is an onerous commitment
Only the next 12 months' portion of the commitment is disclosed — long-term commitments beyond one year are not required disclosures

explanations.a: Non-cancellable purchase commitments that could result in losses must be disclosed. ASC 330-10-50 and ASC 420 address disclosure of purchase commitments — they require both accrual of a probable loss and note disclosure of significant commitments.
explanations.b: The entire future commitment amount ($1 million) is not recognized as a liability — the executory contract (a commitment to purchase in the future) is generally off-balance-sheet under US GAAP unless it is onerous (a loss should be accrued) or meets specific recognition criteria.
explanations.c: Under ASC 330-10-50-5, when a company has a non-cancellable purchase commitment at above-market prices, the loss on the commitment (the unfavorable price differential) should be accrued in the current period when the loss becomes probable and estimable. The $200,000 loss (100,000 units × $2 market price deficiency) should be recognized immediately. The existence and terms of the commitment must also be disclosed in the notes so users can assess future cash obligations.
explanations.d: All significant non-cancellable purchase commitments should be disclosed, including amounts beyond one year. ASC 440 requires disclosure of significant commitments, typically presenting the amounts due in each of the next five years and thereafter.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company's major customer declares bankruptcy on February 5, after the December 31 fiscal year-end but before the financial statements are issued. The customer had an outstanding receivable of $800,000 at December 31 that is now uncollectible. This event should be addressed in the financial statements as

answers.text: Disclosed in a note as a non-adjusting subsequent event only — no adjustment to the December 31 allowance
Disclosed in next year's financial statements only — it occurred after December 31 and does not affect current-year financials
Ignored until the bankruptcy proceedings conclude — the amount of loss cannot be determined until the bankruptcy court makes its determination

An adjusting subsequent event requiring an increase to the allowance for doubtful accounts at December 31 — the bankruptcy provides evidence that the condition (customer's deteriorating financial health) existed at year-end

explanations.a: While note disclosure is also required, this is an adjusting (recognized) subsequent event — it requires actual adjustment of the December 31 balance sheet, not just disclosure. The adjustment reflects that evidence of an existing condition has come to light after year-end.
explanations.b: Financial statements issued after February 5 must reflect events that provide evidence about conditions at December 31. If the customer was already financially distressed at December 31 (which led to bankruptcy so quickly after year-end), the receivable was impaired at year-end.
explanations.c: Waiting for bankruptcy proceedings is not required or appropriate when there is sufficient evidence to estimate the loss. The bankruptcy filing itself is strong evidence of uncollectability.
explanations.d: Under ASC 855-10-55, a Type I (recognized) subsequent event is one that provides additional evidence about conditions that existed at the balance sheet date. If a customer files for bankruptcy shortly after year-end, it typically indicates that the customer's financial deterioration existed at December 31 — the receivable was likely impaired at year-end. The subsequent bankruptcy provides the evidence needed to quantify and record the loss. The allowance for doubtful accounts is adjusted to reduce the receivable to its estimated realizable value as of December 31.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company measures certain financial instruments at fair value using a discounted cash flow model with internally developed assumptions about growth rates, discount rates, and terminal values. Under ASC 820, these measurements are classified as Level

answers.text: Level 1 — because the instruments are regularly valued by the entity's financial modeling team
Level 3 — because the valuation uses significant unobservable inputs (internally developed assumptions) that reflect the entity's own data rather than observable market data
Level 2 — because discounted cash flow models are a standard valuation technique
Level classification is not required for instruments valued using proprietary models — only market-quoted instruments require hierarchy disclosure

explanations.a: Level 1 requires quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities — not a company's internal modeling process. The frequency of the entity's valuation has no bearing on the hierarchy level.
explanations.b: The ASC 820 fair value hierarchy classifies measurements based on the observability of inputs: Level 1 = quoted prices in active markets; Level 2 = observable inputs other than Level 1 prices (market quotes for similar assets, yield curves, market-based inputs); Level 3 = significant unobservable inputs that reflect the entity's own assumptions (internally developed cash flow projections, entity-specific growth rates, entity-selected discount rates not calibrated to observable data). Using a DCF model with internally developed assumptions — where the inputs cannot be observed in active markets — places the measurement in Level 3.
explanations.c: The valuation technique used (DCF vs. market approach vs. income approach) does not determine the hierarchy level — the observability of the inputs determines the level. A DCF using market-observable inputs (e.g., benchmark interest rates, publicly available credit spreads) would be Level 2; using internally developed unobservable inputs makes it Level 3.
explanations.d: ASC 820-10-50 requires all fair value measurements to be classified within the hierarchy and disclosed — including those using proprietary models. The requirement applies universally to recognized and disclosed fair value measurements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A contingent liability for a lawsuit where management believes the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome is 'reasonably possible' and estimates the potential loss between $500,000 and $2,000,000 (with no amount more likely than another within the range). Under ASC 450, the appropriate accounting and disclosure is

answers.text: Accrue $1,250,000 — the midpoint of the range — as the best estimate of the probable loss
Accrue $500,000 — the minimum of the range — and disclose the range
No accrual because the outcome is not probable; disclose the nature of the contingency and the range of possible loss ($500,000 to $2,000,000) in the notes
No disclosure required until the litigation is resolved — contingent liabilities that are 'reasonably possible' need not be disclosed

explanations.a: Accrual requires both a probable outcome AND a reasonably estimable amount. Since the outcome is 'reasonably possible' (not probable), no accrual is made — regardless of the range of estimates.
explanations.b: Accrual at the minimum of the range applies when the loss is probable (not merely reasonably possible) and no single amount within the range is a better estimate than others. Since this contingency is only reasonably possible, no accrual is appropriate.
explanations.c: ASC 450-20-50 establishes: (1) accrue when the loss is probable AND the amount can be reasonably estimated; (2) disclose when the loss is at least reasonably possible. Since this loss is 'reasonably possible' but not 'probable,' no accrual is made. However, disclosure IS required — the notes must describe the nature of the contingency and provide the range of possible loss ($500,000 to $2,000,000). This allows users to assess potential future cash outflows that are not yet recognized.
explanations.d: Reasonably possible contingencies DO require disclosure under ASC 450. Only remote contingencies require neither accrual nor disclosure (though some remote contingencies in certain contexts — like guarantees — still require disclosure).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company changes its inventory costing method from FIFO to weighted-average cost, which is preferable given its homogeneous inventory. Under ASC 250 (Accounting Changes and Error Corrections), how is this change reported?

answers.text: Prospectively — the new method is applied only to inventory purchases after the change date, with no retroactive adjustment

Retrospectively — all prior periods presented are restated to reflect the weighted-average method as if it had always been used, with the cumulative effect reflected as an adjustment to the earliest period's beginning retained earnings
As a prior period error correction — because using FIFO was an error that must be corrected
By recording the cumulative effect of the change as a special charge in the current year's income statement

explanations.a: Changes in accounting principle are not applied prospectively under US GAAP (except for certain specific situations where retrospective application is impracticable). ASC 250 requires retrospective application for voluntary changes in accounting principle.
explanations.b: ASC 250-10-45-5 requires voluntary changes in accounting principle (such as changing from FIFO to weighted-average) to be applied retrospectively to all prior periods presented, as if the new accounting principle had always been used. The cumulative effect on periods before the earliest period presented is reflected as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings (or another appropriate equity component) of the earliest period presented. Prior-period financial statements are restated to reflect the new method.
explanations.c: A change from one acceptable accounting method (FIFO) to another acceptable method (weighted-average) is a change in accounting principle — not an error. Errors involve incorrect applications of GAAP or mathematical mistakes. Changing from one acceptable policy to a preferable one is not an error correction.
explanations.d: The 'catch-up' approach of recording the cumulative effect in the current year's income statement was the previous GAAP treatment (under APB 20) but was eliminated. Current ASC 250 requires full retrospective application — not a current-year cumulative charge.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASU 2016-14, a not-for-profit (NFP) entity must classify its net assets into which categories on the statement of financial position?

answers.text: Permanently restricted, temporarily restricted, and unrestricted — the three-class system from ASC 958
Current net assets and non-current net assets — like for-profit entities
Operating net assets and endowment net assets
Net assets without donor restrictions and net assets with donor restrictions — the two-class system required by ASU 2016-14

explanations.a: The three-class system (permanently restricted, temporarily restricted, unrestricted) was the pre-ASU 2016-14 model under SFAS 117. ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017, simplified the classification to two classes.
explanations.b: NFP entities do not classify net assets as current and non-current in the way for-profit entities classify equity. Net asset classification is donor-restriction based, not liquidity based.
explanations.c: Operating vs. endowment is not the required net asset classification under ASC 958. While endowment funds are an important NFP concept, they are classified within the two-class system based on donor restrictions.
explanations.d: ASU 2016-14 (codified in ASC 958) replaced the previous three-class system with two classes: (1) Net assets without donor restrictions — net assets not subject to donor-imposed stipulations, including board-designated amounts; (2) Net assets with donor restrictions — net assets subject to donor-imposed stipulations that either expire with the passage of time, the fulfillment of a purpose, or that are permanent (endowments). The two-class approach is intended to simplify presentation while still conveying critical information about donor restrictions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: ASU 2016-14 requires NFP entities to provide new disclosures about liquidity. Which of the following BEST describes this requirement?

answers.text: NFPs must present a classified balance sheet separating current and non-current assets and liabilities
NFPs must disclose both qualitative information about how they manage liquid resources and quantitative information about financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditures
NFPs must present a ratio analysis showing the current ratio and quick ratio in the notes
NFPs must obtain an independent liquidity assessment from a registered credit rating agency annually

explanations.a: ASU 2016-14 does not require NFPs to present classified balance sheets. NFPs still present assets and liabilities generally without the current/non-current classification — the liquidity disclosure is in the notes, not on the face of the statement.
explanations.b: ASU 2016-14 requires NFPs to disclose information about the availability and liquidity of their financial assets. This includes: (1) qualitative disclosures — how the organization manages liquidity and liquid resources (e.g., lines of credit available, investment policies, procedures for managing liquidity risk); and (2) quantitative disclosures — the amount of financial assets available at the reporting date to meet cash needs for general expenditures within one year (excluding illiquid assets, board-designated amounts, donor-restricted amounts not available for general use, and other amounts unavailable within one year).
explanations.c: Ratio analysis is not a specific requirement of ASU 2016-14. The qualitative and quantitative narrative disclosures are required — not specific financial ratios.
explanations.d: Independent credit rating agency assessments are not required by ASU 2016-14 or any GAAP standard as part of the financial statement notes.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A donor gives $1,000,000 to a university with the stipulation that the principal must be maintained in perpetuity and that investment earnings may be used only for student scholarships. The $1,000,000 gift is classified in which net asset category on the university's statement of financial position?

answers.text: Net assets without donor restrictions — the donor's gift is unrestricted since the university controls how earnings are spent

Net assets with donor restrictions — the stipulation that principal must be maintained in perpetuity and earnings used only for scholarships represents both a permanent restriction and a purpose restriction
Permanently restricted net assets — classified under the old three-class system, which still applies to endowment gifts
A liability to the donor — the university must return the gift if scholarship programs are ever discontinued

explanations.a: This gift is clearly restricted by donor stipulations — the perpetual maintenance requirement and the purpose restriction for scholarships both impose significant constraints. Classifying it as without donor restrictions would be incorrect.
explanations.b: Under ASU 2016-14 (ASC 958), this gift is classified as net assets with donor restrictions because: (1) the principal is permanently restricted by the donor's requirement that it be maintained in perpetuity (an endowment) — this component will never expire or be released; (2) the investment earnings are restricted by purpose (scholarship use) — these earnings will be reclassified to without donor restrictions when spent on scholarships. The $1,000,000 principal resides permanently in the 'with donor restrictions' category.
explanations.c: The three-class system (permanently restricted, temporarily restricted, unrestricted) was replaced by ASU 2016-14 with the two-class system. The concept of permanent restriction is now subsumed within 'net assets with donor restrictions.'
explanations.d: An endowment gift is not a liability — it is a contribution with restrictions on use. As long as the university complies with the donor's stipulations, there is no repayment obligation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP's board of directors designates $500,000 of unrestricted net assets as a quasi-endowment for long-term investment. How are these assets classified on the NFP's statement of financial position?

answers.text: Net assets without donor restrictions — board designations do not create donor restrictions; the board can remove the designation at any time
Net assets with donor restrictions — any endowment designation creates restrictions regardless of who imposed them
A restricted liability — board-designated amounts are held in trust for specific purposes
A separate line item outside net assets — quasi-endowments are neither restricted nor unrestricted

explanations.a: Under ASC 958-205, only donor-imposed restrictions create 'net assets with donor restrictions.' Board designations — also called quasi-endowments or board-designated endowments — represent the board's discretionary decision to earmark funds for a specific purpose, but because the board itself (not an external donor) imposed the constraint, the designation does not create donor restrictions. The amounts remain classified as net assets without donor restrictions. The board can remove or modify the designation at any time, which fundamentally distinguishes it from a true donor-imposed restriction.
explanations.b: Only restrictions imposed by external donors create 'net assets with donor restrictions.' Internal board actions — no matter how restrictive they appear — do not convert unrestricted net assets to restricted. The key is the source of the restriction: external donor vs. internal board.
explanations.c: Board-designated net assets are equity (net assets), not liabilities. The NFP does not have an obligation to an external party for board-designated amounts.
explanations.d: Board-designated amounts remain within net assets without donor restrictions — they are not presented outside the net asset classification system.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A community foundation has a donor-restricted endowment fund with an original gift of $2,000,000. Due to investment losses, the current fair value of the endowment has declined to $1,700,000 — an 'underwater' endowment. Under ASU 2016-14, how is the $300,000 deficiency classified?

answers.text: Reclassified to net assets without donor restrictions — the deficiency reduces unrestricted net assets as a practical matter
Recorded as a loss in net assets without donor restrictions — only the original gift balance remains in with donor restrictions
Recognized as a liability since the foundation owes the donor the original $2 million
Reported within net assets with donor restrictions — the entire fund balance (including the deficiency) remains in with donor restrictions, and the underwater status must be disclosed separately

explanations.a: The deficiency is not reclassified to net assets without donor restrictions under ASU 2016-14. Previously, some entities reclassified underwater endowment deficiencies to unrestricted net assets, but ASU 2016-14 requires the full endowment balance (including any deficiency) to remain within net assets with donor restrictions.
explanations.b: Recording the loss against net assets without donor restrictions would be incorrect. The underwater endowment balance — even the negative deficiency portion — stays within net assets with donor restrictions.
explanations.c: An underwater endowment does not create a liability to the donor. The NFP is not required to restore the endowment to its original gift amount through additional contributions from other sources. The original donor restriction applies to maintaining the endowment in perpetuity, but market losses are not an obligation payable to the donor.
explanations.d: ASU 2016-14 requires that underwater endowment amounts remain within net assets with donor restrictions — the entire fair value of $1,700,000 is presented within that category. The $300,000 deficiency (the amount by which fair value falls below the original gift amount) must be separately disclosed in the notes, along with the governing board's policy for spending from underwater endowments and any actions taken during the year with respect to such funds.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A university has a permanently restricted endowment of $5,000,000 (original gift). The endowment generates investment returns of $300,000. The donor specified that earnings must be used for graduate fellowships. How are the $300,000 investment returns classified before they are spent?

answers.text: Net assets with donor restrictions — the donor's requirement that earnings be used for graduate fellowships means investment returns are restricted until spent on fellowships
Net assets without donor restrictions — investment returns are always unrestricted regardless of donor specifications on earnings
Added to the permanently restricted principal — investment returns always increase the endowment corpus
Recognized as revenue only when spent on fellowships — income is deferred until the donor's purpose is fulfilled

explanations.a: When a donor specifies how investment earnings from an endowment may be used (for graduate fellowships in this case), those earnings are classified as net assets with donor restrictions until the restriction is met and the funds are spent on fellowships. At that point, the amounts are released from restrictions (reclassified to net assets without donor restrictions as they are spent). The distinction between restricted principal (permanently restricted) and restricted earnings (temporarily restricted by purpose) is important — both reside in 'net assets with donor restrictions' under ASU 2016-14 but for different reasons.
explanations.b: Donor specifications on earnings usage impose purpose restrictions on investment returns. The earnings do not become unrestricted simply because they are income rather than principal.
explanations.c: Investment returns are not automatically added to the endowment corpus (principal). They are either: (1) restricted for specific purposes as specified by the donor (as in this case); (2) available for general purposes if the donor imposed no restrictions on earnings; or (3) in some states, retained in the corpus to maintain purchasing power (UPMIFA provisions). Adding all returns to the corpus would preclude the use of earnings as the donor intended.
explanations.d: Under ASC 958, revenue (including investment income) is recognized when earned — not when spent. The purpose restriction affects classification (with donor restrictions) but not revenue recognition timing.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: ASU 2016-14 introduced enhanced functional expense disclosure requirements for NFPs. Which statement BEST describes what is required?

answers.text: NFPs must present expenses only by natural classification (salaries, rent, supplies) — functional classification is optional
NFPs must present expenses only by functional classification (program services, management and general, fundraising) — natural classification is optional

All NFPs must present an analysis of expenses by both functional and natural classification — either in the statement of activities, a separate statement of functional expenses, or in the notes to financial statements
Only voluntary health and welfare organizations must present the functional expense matrix — other NFPs are exempt from this requirement

explanations.a: Natural classification alone is insufficient. ASU 2016-14 requires both functional and natural classification — not just natural classification.
explanations.b: Functional classification alone was the requirement before ASU 2016-14 for many NFPs. The new standard requires both dimensions.
explanations.c: ASU 2016-14 extended the requirement to present expenses by both functional and natural classification to all NFPs (not just VHWOs as previously required). ASC 958-720-45-15 requires all NFPs to present an analysis of expenses by both: (1) functional classification — program services (disaggregated by program) vs. supporting services (management and general, fundraising, membership development); and (2) natural classification — salaries, occupancy, depreciation, supplies, etc. This analysis may be presented on the face of the financial statements, in a separate statement of functional expenses, or in the notes.
explanations.d: The pre-ASU 2016-14 requirement limited the functional expense matrix to voluntary health and welfare organizations. ASU 2016-14 expanded this requirement to all NFPs — this is one of the significant changes in the standard.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP received $400,000 in cash contributions restricted by donors for a specific program (nutrition education). During the year, the NFP spent $150,000 on the nutrition education program. How is the release from restriction presented in the NFP's financial statements?

answers.text: The $400,000 is recognized as unrestricted revenue when received — conditional receipts are recognized when the condition is met

$150,000 is reclassified from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions (released from restrictions) — the remaining $250,000 remains in net assets with donor restrictions until spent on nutrition education
$400,000 is recognized as unrestricted program revenue when spent — revenue recognition follows spending
The full $400,000 release occurs in the year received — once the NFP has received the funds, it controls them and can release them immediately

explanations.a: These are purpose-restricted contributions (not conditional contributions) — they are recognized as revenue with donor restrictions when received, not as unrestricted revenue. The release from restriction occurs when funds are spent on the designated program.
explanations.b: Under ASC 958-605-45, when a donor restricts a contribution for a specific purpose, the NFP recognizes the contribution as revenue in net assets with donor restrictions. As the NFP spends the funds on the designated purpose, the restriction expires — and a 'release from restriction' is recorded, reclassifying the spent amount from net assets with donor restrictions to net assets without donor restrictions. Spending $150,000 on nutrition education releases $150,000 from restriction; the remaining $250,000 stays restricted until spent on the nutrition program.
explanations.c: Contributions are recognized as revenue when received (for unconditional contributions) — not when spent. The contribution creates revenue in net assets with donor restrictions when received; the spending triggers a reclassification (release from restriction), not additional revenue recognition.
explanations.d: Donor restrictions do not expire simply because the NFP received the funds. Purpose restrictions expire when the designated purpose is fulfilled — receiving cash does not fulfill the purpose restriction.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: The NFP statement of activities reports changes in which net asset categories?

answers.text: Only net assets without donor restrictions — the statement focuses on the operating activities of the organization
Both net assets without donor restrictions AND net assets with donor restrictions — the statement must report the change in each class and in total net assets
Only net assets with donor restrictions — restricted funds are the primary reporting focus for donors and grantors
Retained earnings and additional paid-in capital — NFPs use the same equity categories as for-profit entities

explanations.a: Reporting only the change in net assets without donor restrictions would omit critical information about restricted activity — grant receipts, endowment investment returns, and releases from restriction all affect both net asset categories.
explanations.b: ASC 958-225-45 requires the statement of activities to report the change in net assets for each of the two classes (without donor restrictions and with donor restrictions) as well as the aggregate change in total net assets. Users need both perspectives: the change in unrestricted resources (available for operations) and the change in restricted resources (subject to donor constraints). The statement is the NFP equivalent of the income statement.
explanations.c: Reporting only restricted net assets would provide an incomplete picture — the operations of the organization (expenses, program revenues, unrestricted contributions) primarily affect net assets without donor restrictions.
explanations.d: NFPs have net assets, not retained earnings or APIC — these are for-profit equity concepts. NFP net asset classification is based on the presence or absence of donor-imposed restrictions, not ownership interests.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP receives a $75,000 unconditional cash contribution from a donor who stipulates it must be used for after-school tutoring programs. When and how is this recognized in the statement of activities?

answers.text: As contribution revenue of $75,000 in net assets with donor restrictions when received — because it is unconditional, it is recognized immediately; the purpose restriction means it stays in restricted net assets until the funds are used for tutoring
As deferred revenue until the funds are spent on tutoring programs
As revenue of $75,000 in net assets without donor restrictions when spent on tutoring — cash received before spending creates a refundable advance
As revenue of $75,000 in net assets without donor restrictions when received — all cash contributions are unrestricted until spent

explanations.a: ASC 958-605 establishes that an unconditional contribution is recognized as revenue when received. Because the donor has stipulated use for tutoring, this is a purpose-restricted gift — recognized in net assets with donor restrictions. It remains in that category until the funds are spent on tutoring, at which point a 'release from restriction' is recorded, transferring the amount to net assets without donor restrictions where the expense is also recognized.
explanations.b: Deferred revenue treatment applies to conditional contributions (where conditions have not yet been met) or exchange transactions. An unconditional restricted gift is not deferred — it is revenue in net assets with donor restrictions at the point of receipt.
explanations.c: Recognizing the contribution only when spent is the incorrect timing. Unconditional contributions are recognized as revenue when received — regardless of when the associated expense occurs. The temporal mismatch between recognizing contribution revenue (at receipt) and the related expense (when services are provided) is expected in NFP accounting.
explanations.d: An unconditional restricted contribution is recognized as revenue when received — but in net assets with donor restrictions, not without donor restrictions. The purpose restriction imposed by the donor determines the classification.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP receives a $200,000 conditional contribution — the grant is conditional on the NFP completing 500 hours of community services within 12 months. At the grant date, zero services have been completed. How is this conditional grant recognized?

answers.text: As a refundable advance (liability) of $200,000 until the conditions are substantially met — conditional contributions are not recognized as revenue until the barrier is overcome
As contribution revenue of $200,000 in net assets with donor restrictions — all cash receipts from donors are recognized immediately
As deferred revenue of $200,000, amortized over 12 months as the hours are completed
As contribution revenue of $200,000 in net assets without donor restrictions — conditional contributions are treated as unrestricted pending fulfillment

explanations.a: Under ASU 2018-08 (ASC 958-605), conditional contributions impose a barrier that must be overcome before revenue is recognized. The 500-hour service requirement is a barrier (a specific measurable performance requirement). Until the NFP has substantially met this condition, the $200,000 is recorded as a refundable advance (liability) — not as revenue. As the services are performed, the condition is met and revenue is recognized proportionately. If the NFP fails to meet the condition, the funds must be returned.
explanations.b: Not all cash receipts from donors are immediately recognized as revenue. Conditional contributions require the barrier to be overcome before revenue recognition. The receipt of cash creates a liability (refundable advance) until conditions are met.
explanations.c: Deferred revenue in the exchange transaction sense is not the correct label — the proper term under ASC 958-605 is 'refundable advance' or 'liability for conditional contribution.' The concept is similar, but the classification and terminology matter for NFPs. The amortization approach (recognizing proportionately as hours are completed) is directionally correct for recognizing revenue as the barrier is overcome.
explanations.d: Conditional contributions are not recognized as without-restrictions revenue. They are liabilities until conditions are substantially met — at which point they become restricted or unrestricted revenue depending on whether additional donor restrictions exist.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP spends $120,000 on its environmental education program, using funds received from a donor who restricted the gift for environmental purposes. How is this presented in the statement of activities?

answers.text: As a release from restriction of $120,000 (from net assets with donor restrictions to without donor restrictions) AND as program expenses of $120,000 in net assets without donor restrictions — expenses are always recognized without donor restrictions
As $120,000 in program expenses in net assets with donor restrictions and a simultaneous $120,000 release to net assets without donor restrictions
As a reduction of net assets with donor restrictions of $120,000 — expenses reduce restricted net assets directly
No journal entry is needed until the program is fully completed — partial spending does not trigger recognition

explanations.a: The correct sequence under ASC 958: (1) Release from restriction — record a reclassification that reduces net assets with donor restrictions by $120,000 and increases net assets without donor restrictions by $120,000 (labeled 'Net assets released from restrictions' in the statement of activities); (2) Record the program expense of $120,000 as a decrease in net assets without donor restrictions. This two-step process ensures all expenses appear in the without-restrictions section, while the release from restrictions shows the redeployment of restricted funds. The net effect on total net assets is a decrease of $120,000.
explanations.b: Expenses cannot be classified in net assets with donor restrictions. Presenting program expenses in the restricted category is contrary to ASC 958-225.
explanations.c: Expenses are never recognized in net assets with donor restrictions — all expenses reduce net assets without donor restrictions. When restricted funds are spent on the designated purpose, the process involves a release from restriction (moving funds to without restrictions) followed by expense recognition in the without-restrictions category.
explanations.d: Expenses are recognized when incurred — not only when a program is fully completed. Incremental spending triggers incremental recognition of expenses and releases from restrictions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: In an NFP's statement of activities, all expenses are presented as decreases in

answers.text: Net assets with donor restrictions — expenses reduce the pool of restricted resources available
Net assets without donor restrictions — regardless of the source of funds used to pay for them
The net asset class that matches the source of funds — restricted fund spending reduces restricted net assets
Both net asset classes — expenses are allocated between restricted and unrestricted based on funding source

explanations.a: Expenses are never recognized in net assets with donor restrictions — this is a fundamental principle of NFP accounting under ASC 958-225.
explanations.b: ASC 958-225-45-3 establishes that all expenses of an NFP are classified as decreases in net assets without donor restrictions. Even when an NFP pays for expenses using donor-restricted funds, the mechanism is: (1) first transfer the funds from restricted to unrestricted via a release from restriction; (2) then recognize the expense as a decrease in net assets without donor restrictions. The expense classification is always without donor restrictions — never in the restricted category.
explanations.c: The source of funds does not determine the expense classification. Expenses always reduce net assets without donor restrictions, and the release from restriction mechanism handles the transfer of restricted funds to fund those expenses.
explanations.d: Expenses are not allocated between net asset classes. All expenses, without exception, reduce net assets without donor restrictions — the statement of activities consistently presents expenses in a single classification.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP receives $800,000 in investment returns from its endowment — consisting of $300,000 in dividends and interest, $400,000 in realized gains, and $100,000 in unrealized gains. Investment management fees paid were $50,000. Under ASU 2016-14, how may the NFP present investment returns in the statement of activities?

answers.text: Each component (dividends, realized gains, unrealized gains) must be presented separately — no netting is permitted
The total $800,000 gross is required — netting investment expenses is not permitted

Investment returns may be reported net of related investment expenses — presenting $750,000 net ($800,000 - $50,000); however, the gross income and investment expense amounts must be disclosed in the notes
Only realized returns ($700,000) are reported — unrealized gains are not included in the statement of activities for NFPs

explanations.a: Component-by-component presentation is not required. ASU 2016-14 permits net presentation of investment returns, which is a common and practical reporting approach.
explanations.b: Gross presentation is one option but is not required. The net presentation option is specifically permitted by ASU 2016-14.
explanations.c: ASU 2016-14 (ASC 958-320-45) permits NFPs to present investment returns net of related investment expenses (including management fees, custodial fees, and internal investment management expenses). If net presentation is used: (1) the statement of activities shows $750,000 ($800,000 gross return - $50,000 investment expenses); and (2) the notes must disclose the gross investment return and the investment expenses netted against it, disaggregating the components so users can understand the underlying gross performance. This balance between simplicity on the face and transparency in the notes is the intended approach of ASU 2016-14.
explanations.d: Unrealized gains ARE included in the statement of activities for NFPs — ASC 958-320 requires recognition of both realized and unrealized gains and losses on investments. Excluding unrealized amounts would be incorrect under US GAAP for NFPs.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A law firm donates 200 hours of legal services (at its standard billing rate of $300/hour = $60,000 total) to help an NFP with a contract dispute. The NFP would have hired an attorney if the services had not been donated. How should the NFP account for these donated services?

answers.text: Recognize contribution revenue of $60,000 and program expense of $60,000 — the donated specialized services meet the criteria for recognition
Disclose the donated services in the notes only — in-kind services are never recognized on the face of the financial statements
Recognize contribution revenue of $60,000 and reduce program expenses by $60,000 — services reduce, not increase, expenses
Recognize contribution revenue only when the legal dispute is resolved — uncertainty about the outcome defers recognition

explanations.a: ASC 958-605-25-16 establishes three criteria for recognizing donated services: (1) the services create or enhance non-financial assets, OR (2) the services require specialized skills, are provided by individuals possessing those skills, and would typically need to be purchased if not provided by donation. Legal services requiring specialized skills, provided by licensed attorneys, that the NFP would have otherwise purchased clearly satisfy criterion 2. The NFP recognizes: contribution revenue of $60,000 (increasing net assets) AND legal expense of $60,000 (as a program or supporting service expense). The net effect on total net assets is zero, but both the revenue and expense are grossed up to reflect the economic substance of the transaction.
explanations.b: Donated services that meet the recognition criteria must be recognized on the face of the financial statements — not merely disclosed in notes. Note disclosure alone is insufficient when criteria are met.
explanations.c: The donated services create an expense (legal services were received and consumed) — not a reduction of expenses. Both revenue and expense are recognized separately (gross presentation), not netted.
explanations.d: Recognition is not deferred based on uncertainty about legal outcomes. The services were received and consumed during the year — the contribution and expense are recognized in the period the services are provided.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP museum charges $200 annual membership dues. In return, members receive a 20% discount on gift shop purchases (fair value of this benefit estimated at $50/year) and free admission (regular admission price is $120/year). How should the membership dues be classified?

answers.text: Entirely as contribution revenue of $200 per member — memberships to NFPs are always treated as charitable donations
Entirely as exchange revenue — NFP membership dues are exchange transactions when any benefits are provided
$30 as contribution revenue (the excess of dues over the $170 fair value of benefits received) and $170 as exchange revenue — the portion exceeding the value of benefits received is a contribution
Deferred over 12 months — membership dues are a form of deferred revenue and cannot be recognized at the membership date

explanations.a: Membership dues that include substantial member benefits are not entirely contribution revenue. When members receive benefits (discounts, admission, publications) in return for dues, the exchange portion must be identified and classified separately.
explanations.b: If the dues exceed the fair value of benefits received, the excess represents a contribution — not exchange revenue. Classifying all dues as exchange revenue would understate contribution revenue when dues exceed benefits received.
explanations.c: ASC 958-605 requires bifurcation of membership dues between: (1) exchange revenue — the fair value of benefits received by members ($50 gift shop benefit + $120 admission = $170); and (2) contribution revenue — the excess of dues over the value of benefits received ($200 - $170 = $30). The $30 excess has no direct exchange component — members pay more than the value of benefits received, making the excess a voluntary contribution to the NFP's mission.
explanations.d: Membership dues for a 12-month period may be recognized over the membership year (deferred and amortized) or in full at membership inception depending on the NFP's accounting policy and when the performance obligations are satisfied. However, the split between exchange and contribution components must still be made.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP's statement of cash flows is organized into which sections?

answers.text: Operating activities, program activities, and administrative activities — reflecting the NFP's functional expense categories
Restricted activities and unrestricted activities — mirroring the net asset classification
Operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities — the same structure as for-profit entities
Revenue activities, expense activities, and net asset change activities — specific to the NFP context

explanations.a: Operating, program, and administrative is the functional expense classification — it appears in the statement of activities and the functional expense schedule, not in the statement of cash flows.
explanations.b: The cash flow statement for NFPs is not divided by net asset restriction category. Operating, investing, and financing classification reflects cash flow characteristics — not donor restriction status.
explanations.c: ASC 958-230 requires NFPs to present a statement of cash flows in the same format as for-profit entities under ASC 230 — with three sections: operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. The classification principles are substantially the same, with some NFP-specific considerations (such as treatment of donor-restricted contributions for capital purposes).
explanations.d: Revenue, expense, and net asset change categories describe the structure of the statement of activities — not the statement of cash flows.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP receives $500,000 cash from a donor whose gift is restricted for construction of a new building. How is this cash receipt classified on the NFP's statement of cash flows?

answers.text: Financing activity — donor-restricted contributions for long-lived asset acquisition are classified as financing activities, not operating activities
Operating activity — all contributions from donors are operating activities regardless of restriction
Investing activity — the funds will be used to acquire a capital asset (the building)
Non-cash disclosure — restricted contributions do not appear in the body of the cash flow statement

explanations.a: ASC 958-230-45-11 requires that cash contributions restricted by donors for long-lived asset acquisition (capital additions) be classified as financing activities. The rationale is that such restricted gifts function similarly to long-term financing — they are not available for general operations, are designated for acquiring capital assets, and are comparable to proceeds from long-term debt used to fund capital projects. This differs from unrestricted contributions (classified as operating activities).
explanations.b: Not all contributions are operating activities — the restriction's nature matters. Unrestricted operating contributions are classified as operating; donor-restricted gifts for capital purposes are classified as financing.
explanations.c: The cash receipt from the donor is a financing inflow (from the donor's restricted gift). The subsequent cash payment to build the building would be an investing outflow — the classification of the receipt and the spending are separate events with separate classifications.
explanations.d: The cash was actually received — it is a real cash inflow, not a non-cash transaction. It appears in the body of the statement as a financing inflow.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
