questions.text: An NFP receives $1,000,000 in cash as a permanent endowment gift (principal must be maintained in perpetuity). How is this cash inflow classified on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: Operating activity — donations are operating activities for NFPs
Investing activity — the funds will be invested in the endowment portfolio
Non-cash activity — endowment gifts are not recognized as cash flows
Financing activity — cash received from donors restricted for permanent endowment purposes is classified as a financing inflow, representing long-term capital funding

explanations.a: A permanently restricted endowment gift cannot be used for general operations — it is long-term capital that must be maintained in perpetuity. Classifying it as operating would misrepresent the NFP's operational cash generation.
explanations.b: The investing classification applies to the subsequent investment of the endowment funds (purchasing securities) — not to the receipt of the gift itself. The donor gift is a financing inflow; investing the proceeds is a subsequent investing activity.
explanations.c: The $1,000,000 was received in cash — it is a real cash inflow and must appear in the body of the statement. Only transactions without any cash component are disclosed as non-cash supplemental items.
explanations.d: ASC 958-230 classifies cash received from donors restricted for permanent endowment as a financing activity. This classification reflects that permanent endowment gifts are analogous to long-term equity capital — they are not available for current operations, they represent a perpetual funding commitment, and they increase the NFP's long-term capital base. They are treated similarly to long-term capital contributions in the for-profit context.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under US GAAP, interest paid on borrowings by an NFP is classified on the statement of cash flows as

answers.text: A financing activity — interest relates to debt financing
An operating activity — consistent with the treatment for for-profit entities under ASC 230
An investing activity — interest is the cost of capital deployed in investments
Disclosed as a non-cash supplemental item — interest is an accrual-basis expense only

explanations.a: US GAAP classifies interest paid as an operating activity — not a financing activity. This is counterintuitive (interest relates to debt), but ASC 230 designates interest paid as operating for entities applying US GAAP.
explanations.b: ASC 958-230 applies the same classification principles as ASC 230 for NFPs. Interest paid is classified as an operating activity for NFPs (and for-profit entities) under US GAAP. This uniform treatment means interest paid reduces operating cash flows regardless of the entity's tax-exempt status. (Note: IFRS allows entities to classify interest paid as operating or financing — this flexibility does not exist under US GAAP.)
explanations.c: Interest paid is not an investing activity. Investing activities relate to acquiring and disposing of long-lived assets and investment securities — not to debt servicing costs.
explanations.d: Interest paid is a cash transaction — the actual cash payment for interest is classified and presented in the body of the statement, not as a non-cash supplemental disclosure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP sells equipment for $80,000 cash. The equipment had been donated to the NFP and was restricted by the donor for use in specific programs — the donor specified the asset must be used for educational purposes. The proceeds from the sale are unrestricted. How is the $80,000 classified?

answers.text: Operating activity — the equipment was used in program operations
Financing activity — proceeds from selling donor-contributed assets are financing inflows
Investing activity — the sale of a long-lived asset is an investing activity regardless of whether the original asset was donor-restricted
Non-cash supplemental disclosure only — sales of previously donated assets have no cash flow impact

explanations.a: The classification of cash flows from asset sales is determined by the nature of the asset (long-lived capital asset vs. inventory), not by the asset's use in operations. Capital asset disposals are investing activities.
explanations.b: Proceeds from selling capital assets are investing activities — not financing activities. Financing activities relate to debt and equity transactions, not asset disposals.
explanations.c: ASC 958-230 classifies proceeds from the sale of long-lived assets as investing activities — the same as for for-profit entities. This classification is based on the type of asset disposed of (a capital asset), not on its original source (donor gift) or the restrictions on the original use. The $80,000 proceeds from selling the equipment are an investing inflow.
explanations.d: Cash was actually received ($80,000) — this is a real cash inflow that appears in the body of the statement as an investing inflow. Donated assets that are sold for cash represent actual cash transactions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under the indirect method, an NFP's statement of cash flows starts with the change in net assets. During the year, the NFP received $300,000 in donor-restricted contributions for building construction. This $300,000 was classified as a financing inflow on the cash flow statement. How must it be handled in the operating activities reconciliation?

answers.text: No adjustment needed — restricted contributions are always included in operating activities
No adjustment needed — restricted contributions reduce the change in net assets, so they do not affect operating cash flows

Subtract $300,000 from the change in net assets in the operating section — since this $300,000 was included in the change in net assets (as restricted contribution revenue) but is classified as a financing activity, it must be removed from the operating reconciliation
Add $300,000 to the change in net assets — financing receipts are added back when starting with the change in net assets

explanations.a: Restricted contributions for capital purposes are financing activities — not operating activities. Including them in the operating section without adjustment would misclassify cash flows.
explanations.b: The $300,000 restricted contribution increased the change in net assets (as contribution revenue with donor restrictions). Under the indirect method, the starting point includes this contribution. But because it's classified as financing, it must be removed from the operating activities section to avoid double-counting.
explanations.c: Under the indirect method, the starting point (change in net assets) includes ALL revenues and gains — including the $300,000 restricted contribution, which increased net assets. However, this cash inflow was classified as a financing activity. To reconcile to operating cash flows, the $300,000 must be SUBTRACTED from the operating activities section to remove it — and it simultaneously appears as a $300,000 financing inflow in the financing section. This prevents the same cash from being counted in both operating and financing activities.
explanations.d: Adding the restricted contribution to the operating section would overstate operating cash inflows. The adjustment must subtract it from the operating section, with the corresponding financing inflow in the financing section.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP receives a non-cash gift of publicly traded securities valued at $150,000. The securities are sold immediately for $150,000 cash, and the proceeds are unrestricted (no donor restrictions). How are these transactions reflected on the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: The receipt of securities ($150,000) is an operating inflow; the sale of securities ($150,000) is an investing outflow — the net is zero
Disclosed only as a supplemental non-cash activity of $150,000 — both the gift and the sale are non-cash events
The receipt of donated securities is a non-cash supplemental item ($150,000); the sale of the securities produces a $150,000 investing inflow on the cash flow statement
The $150,000 cash from selling the donated, unrestricted securities is classified as an operating inflow — contributions used in operations are operating cash flows

explanations.a: The combination of a non-cash gift receipt and an investing outflow would net to zero — but the NFP actually received $150,000 in net cash. This approach would misrepresent the actual cash flow.
explanations.b: The sale of the securities produced real cash of $150,000 — this cash flow must appear in the body of the statement, not merely as a non-cash supplemental disclosure. The receipt of the donated securities (non-cash gift) would be disclosed as a non-cash item, but the subsequent sale is a cash transaction.
explanations.c: This represents a common approach — but ASC 958-230 (as interpreted by practice) suggests that when donated securities are immediately converted to cash with no restrictions, the proceeds are generally classified as operating (if unrestricted) or financing (if restricted). The receipt of non-cash donated securities is supplemental; the cash from sale goes in the operating or financing section based on restrictions.
explanations.d: For unrestricted donated securities sold immediately, the cash proceeds are classified as operating activities — reflecting the NFP's receipt of unrestricted resources that support operations. The non-cash gift (receiving the securities) is disclosed as a supplemental non-cash activity to show the economic substance of the original contribution. The proceeds from the sale flow through as operating cash, consistent with how unrestricted cash contributions are classified.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under the indirect method for an NFP, pledges receivable (unconditional promises to give for general operations) increased by $200,000 during the year. How is this change reflected in the statement of cash flows?

answers.text: Added to the change in net assets in the operating section — increasing pledges receivable means more revenue was recognized than cash collected
Subtracted from the change in net assets in the operating section — the increase in receivables means contribution revenue was recognized without cash receipt, overstating the operating cash basis
Classified as an investing activity — pledges receivable are quasi-loans from donors
Disclosed as a non-cash supplemental item — unconditional pledges are not cash until collected

explanations.a: Adding an increase in receivables would further overstate cash inflows. If more revenue was recognized than cash collected (receivables increased), operating cash is LESS than what the change in net assets would suggest — requiring a subtraction, not an addition.
explanations.b: Under the indirect method, working capital changes are applied to reconcile the change in net assets to cash from operations. An increase in pledges receivable means the NFP recognized contribution revenue (increasing net assets) but did not yet collect the cash. This non-cash portion of revenue must be subtracted from the change in net assets to arrive at actual cash receipts from donors. This is analogous to how an increase in accounts receivable is subtracted from net income for for-profit entities.
explanations.c: Pledges receivable are operating receivables — they represent promises from donors to give for general operating purposes. They are not investments or loans — classifying them as investing would be incorrect.
explanations.d: Unconditional pledges are recognized as revenue when made (even before cash is received) under ASC 958-605. The pledge itself is not a cash flow — but the change in the receivable balance is a working capital adjustment in the indirect method. The eventual collection of the pledge will be an operating cash inflow in a future period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASU 2016-14, which information about endowment funds must NFPs disclose in the notes?

answers.text: Only the total endowment balance and the annual payout percentage — no further detail is required
Whether the endowment funds meet UPMIFA requirements — no additional disclosures are needed
The identity of each individual donor who contributed to the endowment — donor privacy notwithstanding

The board's interpretation of applicable law, the endowment spending and investment policies, the composition of endowment funds by net asset class, and information about underwater endowments including aggregate fair value, original gift amount, and aggregate deficiency

explanations.a: The disclosure requirements for endowments under ASU 2016-14 are more extensive than just the balance and payout rate. Users need to understand governance policies, legal interpretations, and the status of individual endowment funds.
explanations.b: UPMIFA compliance is a legal matter — noting compliance alone is insufficient. ASC 958 requires substantive disclosures about the endowment's governance and financial position.
explanations.c: Individual donor identification is not required and would be inappropriate from a donor privacy standpoint. Aggregate information by category is disclosed — not individual donor details.
explanations.d: ASU 2016-14 (ASC 958-205-50) requires NFPs with donor-restricted endowment funds to disclose: (1) the board's interpretation of the relevant laws under which the organization operates (such as UPMIFA) and how that interpretation affects classification of net assets; (2) the organization's endowment spending policy and how it was established; (3) the organization's endowment investment policy; (4) the composition of endowment funds at period end, classified by net asset class; and (5) for underwater endowments — the aggregate fair value of those funds, the aggregate original gift amount (or level required by donor or law), and the aggregate amount of the deficiency.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP received a $500,000 conditional grant. The conditions were substantially met by year-end, and $300,000 of the grant has been recognized as revenue. The remaining $200,000 was not recognized because conditions were not yet met at year-end. What disclosure is required in the notes?

answers.text: No disclosure is required — unrecognized conditional grants are off-balance-sheet and not disclosed

The nature of the unrecognized conditional grant, the total grant amount, and the conditions that have not yet been met — enabling users to understand the potential future revenue and the requirements to earn it
The unrecognized portion ($200,000) is disclosed only in the auditor's report — it is the auditor's responsibility to communicate unrecognized grants
The entire $500,000 grant amount is disclosed as revenue even though $200,000 remains conditional — full grant amounts are always disclosed as if fully earned

explanations.a: Unrecognized conditional contributions are disclosed because they represent significant potential future resources contingent on fulfilling conditions. This information is material to understanding the NFP's expected future funding.
explanations.b: ASC 958-605-50 requires disclosure of the nature, terms, and amounts of conditional contributions that have not yet been recognized as revenue. Users of NFP financial statements need to understand: (1) the nature of the conditions that must still be met; (2) the potential amount of future revenue ($200,000) if conditions are met; (3) the organization's progress toward meeting conditions. This allows donors, grantors, and other stakeholders to assess the NFP's financial prospects and management's ability to fulfill grant conditions.
explanations.c: Conditional grant disclosures are management's responsibility in the notes — not the auditor's communication in the audit report. The auditor evaluates whether disclosures are adequate, but management prepares them.
explanations.d: Only the recognized portion ($300,000) appears as revenue. Disclosing the full $500,000 as revenue before conditions are met would violate the conditional contribution recognition principles of ASC 958-605.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP holds a beneficial interest in a charitable remainder trust. A donor created the trust, naming the NFP as the remainder beneficiary (to receive trust assets upon the donor's death). What must the NFP disclose about this split-interest agreement?

answers.text: The existence of the arrangement, the nature of the split-interest agreement (charitable remainder trust), the basis for determining the value of the NFP's beneficial interest, and any significant uncertainties about the arrangement
Nothing — the trust assets are not the NFP's and do not appear on the balance sheet until the donor dies
The arrangement is only disclosed if the trust assets exceed $1,000,000 — below that threshold, split-interest agreements are immaterial
Only if the trust uses a third-party trustee — trustee-managed trusts require different disclosure

explanations.a: ASC 958-30 requires NFPs to disclose information about split-interest agreements (including charitable remainder trusts, charitable lead trusts, gift annuities, and pooled income funds). Required disclosures include: the nature of the activities conducted under the agreements, the basis for measuring the beneficial interest, any uncertainties about the realization of the expected benefit, and the amount of the beneficial interest recognized. This allows users to understand the nature, timing, and reliability of future expected receipts.
explanations.b: The NFP actually DOES recognize its beneficial interest in the charitable remainder trust on the balance sheet — the actuarially determined present value of the future remainder interest is recognized as an asset and as contribution revenue (with donor restrictions) when the trust is established. The arrangement and the recognized asset require disclosure.
explanations.c: There is no dollar threshold in ASC 958-30 below which split-interest agreements are exempt from disclosure. Materiality applies, but it is a judgment-based threshold — not a fixed $1,000,000 cutoff.
explanations.d: The trustee arrangement affects which entity holds the trust assets, but disclosure requirements under ASC 958-30 apply to all split-interest agreements with a beneficial interest, regardless of trustee arrangements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASU 2016-14, NFPs that allocate costs among functional categories must disclose

answers.text: The names and compensation of all employees whose salaries are allocated across functions
The total amount of management and general expenses as a percentage of total expenses — this percentage must be below 15% to maintain tax-exempt status
The methods used to allocate costs that benefit more than one functional category — such as how occupancy costs, depreciation, and employee time are allocated between program and supporting services
A detailed schedule of all occupancy costs including lease terms and square footage — functional allocation note requires real property disclosure

explanations.a: Individual employee names and compensation are not required to be disclosed in the functional expense allocation note. Compensation data appears in the functional expense matrix (salary, wages category) — but not individual names and amounts in the note.
explanations.b: The 15% threshold is not a GAAP requirement. There is no GAAP-mandated ratio of supporting services to total expenses. Tax-exemption requirements and public charity tests may have separate ratios, but these do not determine GAAP note disclosures.
explanations.c: ASU 2016-14 (ASC 958-720-45-15 and 50-1) requires that when costs are allocated among functional categories, the NFP must disclose the method or methods used to make those allocations. This is important because cost allocation affects the distribution of expenses between program services and supporting services — which users rely on to evaluate organizational efficiency. Common methods include: allocating salaries based on time studies or estimates; allocating occupancy based on square footage; allocating telecommunications based on usage — and the methods chosen can materially affect the functional expense presentation.
explanations.d: Real property disclosure (lease terms, square footage) is not a specific requirement of the functional expense allocation note. Square footage may be referenced as an allocation method, but detailed lease schedule disclosure is not required in this context.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: In preparing the quantitative liquidity disclosure under ASU 2016-14, an NFP has total financial assets of $5,000,000 as of year-end. However, $2,000,000 is in the endowment (board-designated for long-term investment), $500,000 is donor-restricted for a multi-year capital campaign, and $300,000 is subject to a 90-day withdrawal restriction from an investment fund. What amount of financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditures should be disclosed?

answers.text: $5,000,000 — total financial assets regardless of restrictions or availability
$3,000,000 — total less the endowment (board-designated amounts excluded)
$2,500,000 — total less the endowment and the donor-restricted capital campaign funds

$2,200,000 — total financial assets ($5,000,000) less the board-designated endowment ($2,000,000), the donor-restricted capital campaign funds ($500,000), and the investment fund with the 90-day withdrawal restriction ($300,000) — only assets actually available within one year for general expenditures

explanations.a: Disclosing total financial assets without reduction for unavailable amounts would overstate liquidity and mislead users about the NFP's actual capacity to meet operating obligations.
explanations.b: Excluding only the endowment still overstates liquidity — the donor-restricted capital campaign funds and the investment fund with a withdrawal restriction are also unavailable for general expenditures within one year.
explanations.c: Excluding the endowment and capital campaign funds but not the illiquid investment fund still overstates available liquidity — the 90-day restriction means the $300,000 is not freely available within one year for general expenditures.
explanations.d: The quantitative liquidity disclosure under ASU 2016-14 (ASC 958-210-50) requires disclosure of financial assets available within one year to meet general expenditure needs. Amounts must be excluded if they are: (1) board-designated or board-restricted — the $2,000,000 quasi-endowment is not available for general use without board action; (2) donor-restricted — the $500,000 capital campaign funds are restricted by donors for a specific purpose and not available for general operations; (3) subject to contractual restrictions limiting availability — the $300,000 with a 90-day withdrawal restriction is not freely accessible within one year (or the restriction creates a practical availability concern). $5,000,000 - $2,000,000 - $500,000 - $300,000 = $2,200,000.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP hospital has board members who also serve as executives of a major pharmaceutical supplier that sells $3 million of drugs to the hospital annually. The board members recuse themselves from vendor selection votes. Under GAAP, what disclosure is required?

answers.text: No disclosure — the recusal process satisfies independence requirements and eliminates any disclosure obligation

Disclosure of the related party relationship and transaction as required by ASC 850 — the nature of the relationship, description of the transaction, amounts involved ($3 million), and any amounts payable to the related parties at year-end
Disclosure only if the transactions were not at arm's length — at-market transactions with related parties need not be disclosed
Disclosure in a special 'governance' note required only for tax-exempt hospitals — general-purpose NFPs are not required to disclose board member business relationships

explanations.a: Recusal from votes is a governance process — it does not eliminate the GAAP disclosure requirement. Related party transactions must be disclosed in the financial statement notes regardless of whether conflicts were procedurally managed.
explanations.b: ASC 850 applies to all entities, including NFPs. Board members who also have executive roles in a significant supplier are related parties — the board relationship creates the related-party connection. The $3 million annual supplier relationship with related parties must be disclosed including: the nature of the relationship (board member is an executive of the supplier); a description of the transaction (drug purchases); the dollar amount ($3 million annually); and amounts payable to the related party at year-end. The recusal process may be disclosed as part of the governance context, but it does not eliminate the disclosure requirement.
explanations.c: GAAP does not have an exemption from related-party disclosure when transactions are at market prices. The relationship itself creates disclosure obligations — the arm's-length nature affects the extent of disclosure context, not whether disclosure is required.
explanations.d: ASC 850 applies to all GAAP reporters — including NFPs. There is no special carve-out for general-purpose NFPs or limited disclosure to hospitals only.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A university has unrelated business income from its parking garage operations. The university's management determines that a tax position regarding the allocation of costs to the parking operation results in a beneficial tax outcome. When evaluating uncertain tax positions, the university applies which recognition and measurement standard?

answers.text: NFPs are completely exempt from ASC 740 (Income Taxes) — no uncertain tax position analysis is required
The university applies the more-likely-than-not recognition threshold — a tax position is recognized if there is greater than 50% likelihood of being sustained on examination

NFPs apply ASC 740-10 for uncertain tax positions — the recognition threshold is 'more likely than not,' and the measurement reflects the largest amount of benefit that is more than 50% likely of being realized upon settlement
NFPs use a 'probable' threshold (greater than 75%) for uncertain tax positions — more conservative than for-profit entities

explanations.a: NFPs with unrelated business income (UBI) are subject to income taxes on that UBI. Even tax-exempt organizations have uncertain tax positions to evaluate — for UBI-related positions, for payroll taxes, or potentially for their overall tax-exempt status if operations have drifted from the exempt purpose.
explanations.b: This partially describes the recognition threshold correctly but misidentifies the measurement approach — measurement requires recognizing the largest amount that is more than 50% likely of being realized, which may differ from simply whether recognition occurs.
explanations.c: ASC 740-10 (Accounting for Uncertainty in Income Taxes) applies to all entities, including NFPs, that have any income tax uncertainty to evaluate. The two-step approach requires: (1) Recognition — the tax position must be more likely than not (>50% probability) of being sustained upon examination by the taxing authority; (2) Measurement — the amount recognized is the largest amount of tax benefit that is more than 50% likely of being realized upon ultimate settlement. For the university's UBI cost allocation position, it must assess whether the position meets the more-likely-than-not threshold and, if so, measure the benefit at the largest amount meeting the >50% probability standard.
explanations.d: There is no 75% threshold in ASC 740. The recognition threshold is more-likely-than-not (>50%), and the measurement is also based on the >50% likelihood of realization standard.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An NFP community center received 5,000 volunteer hours from community residents helping with administrative tasks, plus 200 hours of legal advice from a volunteer attorney (who typically charges $400/hour and whose services the NFP would otherwise have purchased). How should the notes address these contributions?

answers.text: Both types of volunteer service must be recognized as contribution revenue and expense in the financial statements, with note disclosure of the amount and nature
Neither type of volunteer service is recognized — volunteer services are never recognized under ASC 958-605
Neither is required to be disclosed — routine volunteer services and professional services are both at management's discretion

Only the legal services meet the recognition criteria and are recognized ($80,000 revenue and expense); the volunteer administrative hours are not recognized but may be described qualitatively in the notes; the notes disclose the nature and extent of recognized contributed services and the programs supported

explanations.a: Only specialized services meeting the recognition criteria are recognized — routine volunteer administrative services do not meet the ASC 958-605 criteria (they do not require specialized skills). Recognizing all volunteer hours would violate the standard.
explanations.b: Contributed services that require specialized skills and would otherwise be purchased ARE recognized. The attorney's services clearly qualify — ASC 958-605-25-16 requires recognition. Saying neither type is recognized is incorrect.
explanations.c: Disclosures about recognized contributed services are required — not merely optional. The nature, extent, and programs supported by recognized contributed services must be disclosed.
explanations.d: ASC 958-605-25-16 establishes that contributed services requiring specialized skills (provided by someone with those skills) that the NFP would otherwise purchase must be recognized. The 200 hours of legal advice at $400/hour = $80,000 meets all criteria and is recognized as contribution revenue and as expense. The 5,000 volunteer administrative hours do not require specialized skills — they are not recognized. The notes must disclose: (1) the nature and extent of the recognized contributed services (legal, 200 hours, $80,000) and the programs they supported; (2) qualitatively, the NFP may describe the significant volunteer contribution of the administrative hours even though not recognized, to communicate the breadth of community support.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: State and local government financial reporting under GASB uses two distinct perspectives. Which statement correctly describes these two perspectives?

answers.text: Government-wide statements use the economic resources measurement focus and accrual basis; governmental fund statements use the current financial resources measurement focus and modified accrual basis
Government-wide statements use the current financial resources measurement focus; governmental fund statements use the full economic resources measurement focus
All governmental financial statements use the modified accrual basis — the two perspectives differ only in the funds included
Government-wide statements use the cash basis; governmental fund statements use the accrual basis

explanations.a: GASB 34 established a dual reporting model for state and local governments. Government-wide financial statements present a comprehensive, long-term view of the government's financial position using the economic resources measurement focus (tracking all economic resources, including capital assets and long-term obligations) and accrual basis of accounting (recognizing revenues when earned and expenses when incurred). Governmental fund financial statements present a shorter-term, fiscal accountability perspective using the current financial resources measurement focus (tracking only liquid, near-term financial resources) and modified accrual basis (recognizing revenues when measurable and available; expenditures when liabilities are incurred for most items).
explanations.b: This reverses the descriptions. Government-wide statements use economic resources (the broader, long-term perspective); governmental fund statements use current financial resources (the shorter-term perspective).
explanations.c: Not all governmental statements use modified accrual. Government-wide statements use full accrual; proprietary fund statements also use full accrual. Only governmental fund statements use modified accrual.
explanations.d: Cash basis accounting is not used in GASB financial reporting. Cash basis would not reflect the government's full financial position or the cost of services provided.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: Under the modified accrual basis used for governmental funds, revenues are recognized when they are

answers.text: Received in cash — modified accrual requires cash receipt before revenue recognition
Legally due — revenues are recognized when the government has a legal right to collect them
Earned by the government — the same as full accrual basis; 'modified' refers only to expenditures
Both measurable (can be reasonably estimated) AND available (expected to be collected within the current period or within 60 days after year-end to finance current-period expenditures)

explanations.a: Modified accrual is not the same as cash basis — revenues are recognized before cash is received if the measurable and available criteria are met. Property taxes, for example, are recognized when levied (before collection) if the availability criteria are met.
explanations.b: Legal due date alone does not trigger recognition — the availability criterion (expected collection within the current period or within 60 days) must also be met. A legally due but uncollectible or uncollected amount does not meet the modified accrual standard.
explanations.c: Modified accrual differs from full accrual precisely in revenue recognition — the 'available' criterion does not exist under full accrual. 'Modified' refers to revenue recognition (adding the availability requirement) as well as certain expenditure timing differences.
explanations.d: Under GASB standards, governmental fund revenues are recognized when they are measurable (the amount can be reasonably determined) and available (expected to be collected in time to pay current period obligations — generally within 60 days after the fiscal year end for most revenues). Property taxes collected within 60 days of year-end are available; taxes expected to be collected after 60 days are deferred to the next period. This availability limitation reflects the governmental fund's focus on current financial resources.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: Under modified accrual, when are expenditures recognized in governmental funds for most items?

answers.text: When cash is paid — expenditures are not recognized until the government cuts the check
When the fund liability is incurred — generally when goods or services are received, creating an obligation to pay
When the budget is approved — government expenditures follow the appropriation timeline
When paid from the bank account — electronic disbursements trigger expenditure recognition

explanations.a: Modified accrual expenditure recognition is not strictly cash basis — expenditures are recognized when the liability is incurred, not when cash is disbursed. There may be a timing difference between incurring the obligation and making the payment.
explanations.b: GASB standards require governmental funds to recognize expenditures in the accounting period when the fund liability is incurred — generally when goods or services are received and a legal obligation to pay arises. This is similar to expense recognition under accrual accounting for most transactions. The key distinction from full accrual is that governmental funds do not recognize long-term liabilities (such as pension obligations or bonds payable) as fund expenditures when incurred — instead, debt service expenditures are recognized when due.
explanations.c: Budget appropriation does not trigger expenditure recognition. Budgetary accounting and GAAP accounting are separate systems in government. An appropriation authorizes spending but does not create an accounting expenditure.
explanations.d: The disbursement date is not the recognition date for expenditures. Expenditures are recognized when the liability is incurred — which precedes the payment date.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: A city's water utility is operated as an enterprise fund. The basis of accounting for the enterprise fund's financial statements is

answers.text: Modified accrual — all government funds use modified accrual
Cash basis — utility operations are reported on a cash flow basis
Budgetary basis — enterprise funds report on the budgetary basis for accountability
Full accrual (economic resources measurement focus) — proprietary funds use the same basis as for-profit business entities because they operate similarly to businesses

explanations.a: Modified accrual is used only for governmental funds (general fund, special revenue, capital projects, debt service, permanent). Proprietary funds use full accrual.
explanations.b: Cash basis is not a GAAP basis for governmental financial reporting. Enterprise funds use full accrual — recognizing revenues when earned and expenses when incurred.
explanations.c: Budgetary basis is used for budgetary comparison schedules — not for the fund financial statements. GAAP basis (full accrual for proprietary funds) governs the fund statements.
explanations.d: GASB requires proprietary funds (enterprise funds and internal service funds) to use the economic resources measurement focus and full accrual basis of accounting — essentially the same basis as for-profit entities. Enterprise funds are designed to operate like businesses (charging fees for services), so their financial statements resemble business financial statements. Revenues are recognized when earned (water usage revenue accrued based on consumption), and all economic resources (including capital assets and long-term debt) are reflected in the fund's financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: Under GASB 34, which fund is ALWAYS presented as a major governmental fund?

answers.text: The debt service fund — debt management is the primary obligation of all governments
The capital projects fund — capital expenditures represent the most significant government activities
The general fund — it is the primary operating fund and always a major fund regardless of size
All governmental funds are always major — GASB 34 eliminated the distinction between major and non-major funds

explanations.a: Debt service funds are not automatically major funds. They meet the major fund criteria only if they satisfy the 10%/5% quantitative thresholds or are designated major by government officials.
explanations.b: Capital projects funds are not automatically major. They satisfy the major fund criteria only when they meet the quantitative size thresholds.
explanations.c: GASB 34 paragraph 76 establishes that the general fund is ALWAYS reported as a major fund — regardless of its relative size. The general fund is the primary operating fund of a government, used to account for all activities not accounted for in other funds. Its universal major fund status reflects its fundamental importance to users' understanding of the government's financial position and operations.
explanations.d: GASB 34 maintained the distinction between major and non-major funds. Only the general fund (plus any enterprise fund) that meets size criteria, or funds designated by government officials, are reported as major funds. Other funds are aggregated in the 'Other Governmental Funds' or 'Other Enterprise Funds' columns.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: A reconciliation is required between governmental fund financial statements and government-wide financial statements. Which of the following represents a common reconciling item?

answers.text: Capital assets are reported in the government-wide statements but not in governmental fund statements — the acquisition is recorded as an expenditure in the funds but as an asset on the government-wide balance sheet, requiring addition to reconcile from fund balance to net position
Cash is reported in the fund statements but not in the government-wide statements — cash is a current resource that belongs only in fund reporting
Long-term debt is reported in the governmental fund statements — the reconciliation removes it for government-wide reporting
No reconciliation items are necessary because GASB designed the dual reporting system to produce identical fund and government-wide balances

explanations.a: GASB 34 requires a reconciliation between governmental fund financial statements (current financial resources, modified accrual) and government-wide financial statements (economic resources, full accrual). Capital assets are a major reconciling item: in governmental fund statements, capital asset purchases are recorded as EXPENDITURES (reducing fund balance); in government-wide statements, the same purchases are recorded as ASSETS (which are then depreciated). The reconciliation adds back the capital assets (net of accumulated depreciation) to convert from fund balance to government-wide net position. Other common reconciling items include: long-term liabilities (in government-wide but not in funds); revenues deferred under the 60-day availability rule (deferred in funds, recognized in government-wide); and internal service fund assets.
explanations.b: Cash is reported in both fund statements and government-wide statements — it is not a reconciling item. Cash is a current resource in fund statements and also a current asset in the government-wide statement of net position.
explanations.c: Long-term debt is in the government-wide statements (not governmental fund statements) — the reconciliation adds the long-term debt as a reduction, not a removal. The fund statements do not report long-term liabilities; the government-wide statements do.
explanations.d: The dual reporting system intentionally produces different results — fund balance and government-wide net position differ significantly. The reconciliation (required in both the balance sheet and the statement of revenues, expenditures, and changes in fund balance) explains these differences.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: A county issues $10 million in general obligation bonds. In the debt service fund (governmental fund), the issuance is recorded as

answers.text: A $10 million liability — debt service funds record long-term liabilities just like enterprise funds
A $10 million non-operating gain — bond proceeds are gains from debt financing
A $10 million expenditure — all financing activities reduce fund balance in governmental funds
A $10 million other financing source — proceeds from long-term debt are 'other financing sources' in governmental fund accounting, not revenues or liabilities on the fund balance sheet

explanations.a: Long-term liabilities are NOT recognized in governmental fund statements. The current financial resources measurement focus means the fund recognizes only current assets, current liabilities, and deferred inflows/outflows. Long-term debt appears as a liability only in the government-wide statement of net position.
explanations.b: Bond proceeds are not revenues or gains in governmental fund accounting. They are classified as 'other financing sources' — a separate category from revenues that includes bond issuance proceeds, transfers in, and interfund loans.
explanations.c: The issuance of bonds is not an expenditure. Expenditures in governmental fund accounting represent outflows of current financial resources for services, goods, or debt service payments. Bond issuance increases current financial resources (cash) — it is an inflow, not an outflow.
explanations.d: GASB standards require that proceeds from long-term debt issuances be reported as 'other financing sources' in governmental fund statements — separate from revenues. The statement of revenues, expenditures, and changes in fund balance includes a section for 'Other Financing Sources and Uses' where bond proceeds appear. This separates routine operating revenues from financing inflows. In the government-wide statements, the bond issuance creates a long-term liability and is reflected as an increase in cash and a corresponding increase in long-term debt.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government measurement focus and basis of accounting
questions.text: A city's general fund purchases equipment for $500,000. In the general fund financial statements, this transaction is recorded as a $500,000 expenditure. In the government-wide financial statements, the same transaction produces a different result. What is the government-wide treatment?

answers.text: The equipment purchase is also recorded as a $500,000 expenditure in the government-wide statements — the treatment is identical to the governmental fund

The equipment is recorded as a $500,000 capital asset in the government-wide statement of net position and is depreciated over its useful life — the government-wide expense is annual depreciation, not the full $500,000 at purchase
The equipment purchase is not recorded in the government-wide statements — capital assets are excluded from government-wide reporting
The equipment is recorded as a $500,000 prepaid asset in the government-wide statements and expensed over five years regardless of actual useful life

explanations.a: The treatment differs significantly between the governmental fund and government-wide statements — this is one of the key purposes of the dual reporting model and the required reconciliation.
explanations.b: Under the economic resources measurement focus and full accrual basis used in government-wide statements, capital asset acquisitions are capitalized and depreciated. The $500,000 equipment purchase is recorded as a capital asset in the government-wide statement of net position, and annual depreciation expense (based on the asset's useful life) is recognized in the government-wide statement of activities. This contrasts with the governmental fund's $500,000 expenditure recognized at purchase — the reconciliation between fund statements and government-wide statements adds back the $500,000 expenditure and substitutes the net book value of the capital asset and the period's depreciation expense.
explanations.c: Capital assets are specifically included in government-wide reporting — this is one of the key differences from governmental fund reporting. The government-wide statement of net position presents the government's full economic position including all capital assets.
explanations.d: Capital assets are depreciated over their actual useful lives (or estimated useful lives) under GASB 34 — not over a standardized 5-year period. The depreciation method (straight-line, declining balance, etc.) and useful life estimate follow reasonable accounting principles consistent with the nature of the asset.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: The General Fund of a state or local government is BEST described as

answers.text: The fund used exclusively for major capital asset acquisition and construction projects
The fund that accumulates resources for repayment of general long-term debt
The primary operating fund that accounts for all financial resources not required to be reported in another fund
The fund that accounts for pension and employee benefit obligations

explanations.a: Capital asset acquisition is accounted for in the Capital Projects Fund — not the General Fund, though small capital purchases may pass through the General Fund.
explanations.b: Accumulating resources for long-term debt repayment is the purpose of the Debt Service Fund.
explanations.c: The General Fund is the primary operating fund of state and local governments. It accounts for all government activities not required to be accounted for in another fund — including general government operations, public safety, parks, and other core services financed primarily by taxes and fees. Every governmental entity has a General Fund, and GASB 34 requires it always to be reported as a major fund.
explanations.d: Pension and employee benefit obligations are accounted for in Pension Trust Funds (fiduciary funds) — not in the General Fund.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A county uses a fund to account for state highway grant revenues legally restricted to road maintenance activities. This fund is MOST likely a

answers.text: Capital Projects Fund — road maintenance involves capital assets
Special Revenue Fund — revenues legally restricted or committed for specific operating purposes other than debt service or capital projects
General Fund — all government revenues are initially deposited in the General Fund
Debt Service Fund — restricted grant revenues reduce future borrowing needs

explanations.a: Capital Projects Funds account for resources used for major capital asset acquisition or construction — not ongoing maintenance operations. Road maintenance is an operating activity unless it constitutes a significant improvement extending asset life.
explanations.b: A Special Revenue Fund accounts for proceeds of specific revenue sources that are legally restricted or committed for specified purposes other than debt service or capital projects. State highway grant revenues legally restricted for road maintenance represent exactly this type of arrangement — a Special Revenue Fund is required to demonstrate compliance with the legal restriction and to prevent commingling with general revenues.
explanations.c: Revenues legally restricted for specific purposes cannot be commingled with General Fund revenues — the legal restriction itself requires separate fund accounting.
explanations.d: Debt Service Funds accumulate resources for principal and interest payments on general long-term debt — they have no connection to operating grant revenues restricted for maintenance activities.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A city operates a water utility that charges residential and business customers user fees designed to cover all operating costs, capital improvements, and debt service. The water utility should be accounted for in

answers.text: The General Fund — all city operations are accounted for in the General Fund unless specifically required otherwise
An Enterprise Fund — the utility charges fees to external users to finance its costs, making it business-like in nature
A Debt Service Fund — the water utility has revenue bonds outstanding
A Special Revenue Fund — water fees are restricted revenues

explanations.a: GASB 34 requires (or permits) Enterprise Funds for business-type activities charging fees to external users. Using the General Fund for a major utility operation would obscure the utility's economic performance and its ability to sustain itself from user fees.
explanations.b: GASB 34 requires or permits Enterprise Funds when activities are financed primarily through fees charged to external users. The city water utility meets the primary criteria: fees charged to external customers (residents and businesses) are designed to recover the full cost of service. Enterprise Funds use full accrual accounting to reflect the self-sustaining, business-like nature — including capital assets, long-term debt, and cost of services.
explanations.c: While the water utility may have revenue bonds, Debt Service Funds handle repayment of general long-term debt. Revenue bonds tied to enterprise operations are accounted for within the Enterprise Fund itself.
explanations.d: Special Revenue Funds use modified accrual and are for restricted operating revenues — not for self-sustaining business-like activities with capital asset tracking and long-term debt that require full accrual accounting.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A state receives a $2 million bequest with the requirement that the principal be maintained in perpetuity and only investment earnings be used for state public library programs. This bequest should be accounted for in

answers.text: A Permanent Fund — the principal is legally restricted to investment in perpetuity, and only earnings (for government programs) may be expended
A Special Revenue Fund — the investment earnings are restricted for library use
A Private-Purpose Trust Fund — the citizen's charitable intent benefits the community
The General Fund — the state government receives and controls the assets

explanations.a: A Permanent Fund (a type of governmental fund) is specifically designed for resources where: (1) the corpus (principal) is legally restricted so it must remain intact in perpetuity; and (2) only the investment earnings may be expended; and (3) the earnings must support government programs or citizens. This bequest satisfies all three criteria — it is the textbook Permanent Fund scenario.
explanations.b: While the earnings are restricted for library use, the perpetual nature of the principal restriction places this in a Permanent Fund rather than a Special Revenue Fund. The Special Revenue Fund would not capture the permanent principal restriction.
explanations.c: Private-Purpose Trust Funds are for trust arrangements that benefit individuals, organizations, or other governments (not the reporting government's own programs). The library system is a government program — not a private beneficiary — so a Permanent Fund applies.
explanations.d: The General Fund cannot hold permanently restricted principal — the legal restriction requires separate fund accounting to prevent commingling and to demonstrate compliance.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A county's central services department provides IT support, fleet maintenance, and printing to all county departments on a cost-reimbursement basis. Departments pay for these services based on usage. This operation should be accounted for in

answers.text: The General Fund — central services departments support General Fund activities and should be consolidated there
A Special Revenue Fund — the cost-reimbursement charges are restricted revenues for central services
An Internal Service Fund — the activity provides services primarily to other government departments on a cost-reimbursement basis
An Enterprise Fund — the county charges fees for services regardless of whether the users are internal or external

explanations.a: Using the General Fund would obscure the costs of central services and prevent meaningful cost allocation to user departments. The Internal Service Fund structure enables transparent, accurate cost allocation.
explanations.b: Special Revenue Funds account for external restricted revenues — not internal charging arrangements between government departments. The cost-reimbursement nature is a hallmark of an Internal Service Fund, not a Special Revenue Fund.
explanations.c: Internal Service Funds are used when a government activity provides goods or services to other funds, departments, or agencies of the same government primarily on a cost-reimbursement basis. The central services department serves internal county departments — IT, fleet, printing — and charges them based on usage at rates designed to recover costs. This is the classic Internal Service Fund scenario, enabling efficient cost allocation and management accountability for shared services.
explanations.d: Enterprise Funds require that services be provided primarily to external users (outside the government) who pay fees. The central services department serves internal departments — not the public or external customers. If the county began providing IT services to outside entities commercially, an Enterprise Fund would become appropriate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A state acts as a collection agent for sales tax revenues belonging to municipalities. The state collects, temporarily holds, and then distributes the taxes to cities and counties. The state has no administrative involvement and no discretion over the funds. This arrangement is accounted for in

answers.text: A Special Revenue Fund — tax revenue collected for other governments is restricted
A Private-Purpose Trust Fund — the municipalities are the beneficiaries of the tax distributions
The General Fund — all tax collections pass through the state's General Fund
A Custodial Fund — the state holds assets purely in a custodial capacity, acting as agent with no administrative involvement, disbursing amounts to the appropriate governments

explanations.a: Special Revenue Funds account for the state's own restricted revenues — not assets the state holds in custody for other governments.
explanations.b: Private-Purpose Trust Funds involve formal trust arrangements with administrative involvement and management of assets for specific beneficiaries. Here the state is simply a pass-through collection agent with no discretion — a trust arrangement is not present.
explanations.c: Commingling municipal tax revenues with the state's General Fund would be inappropriate — those assets belong to the municipalities, not the state.
explanations.d: GASB 84 established Custodial Funds (which replaced Agency Funds) for resources that a government holds and administers in a purely custodial capacity. The key characteristic is that the government has no administrative involvement — it simply receives and passes through resources to their rightful owners. The state collecting and immediately distributing municipal sales tax revenues, with no investment or management discretion, is a textbook Custodial Fund situation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A city's General Fund transfers $8 million to its Capital Projects Fund to help finance construction of a new library. In the governmental fund financial statements, this interfund transfer is reported as

answers.text: Revenue of $8 million in the Capital Projects Fund and expenditure of $8 million in the General Fund
A loan receivable of $8 million in the General Fund and loan payable in the Capital Projects Fund
Deferred revenue in the Capital Projects Fund until the library is completed and opens
An other financing use of $8 million in the General Fund and an other financing source of $8 million in the Capital Projects Fund

explanations.a: Classifying interfund transfers as revenues and expenditures would inflate both amounts — making the General Fund appear to have made a $8 million expenditure (reducing its operating results) and the Capital Projects Fund appear to have earned $8 million in new revenues. Both mischaracterize the economic substance of a non-reciprocal internal movement.
explanations.b: Interfund transfers are not loans — they are non-reciprocal flows with no expectation of repayment. Interfund loans (with repayment terms) would be reported as interfund receivables and payables. This transfer has no repayment expectation.
explanations.c: Deferred revenue applies to exchange transactions where revenue recognition is deferred pending performance. An interfund transfer is not an exchange — it is an internal movement between the same government's funds, with no deferred recognition concept applicable.
explanations.d: GASB standards require interfund transfers (non-reciprocal movements of resources between funds, without expectation of repayment) to be reported as: Other Financing Uses in the fund providing resources and Other Financing Sources in the fund receiving resources. This presentation: (1) keeps transfers separate from revenues and expenditures, preserving the integrity of each fund's operating results; (2) shows total resource flows across all funds; and (3) allows users to distinguish between operating revenues/expenditures and internal capital reallocations.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: state and local government purpose of funds
questions.text: A government has the following funds: General Fund, two Special Revenue Funds, a Capital Projects Fund, a Debt Service Fund, an Enterprise Fund, and an Internal Service Fund. Under GASB 34's major fund reporting requirements, which of the following is CORRECT?

answers.text: All seven funds must be individually reported as major funds — GASB 34 requires separate reporting for every fund
Only the General Fund and Enterprise Fund are always major funds — other funds are never major
Only the General Fund and the Capital Projects Fund are automatically major — other funds depend on their financial size

The General Fund is always a major fund; other governmental funds and the Enterprise Fund are major if they meet the 10%/5% quantitative thresholds — funds that do not qualify are aggregated in 'Other Governmental Funds' and 'Other Enterprise Funds' columns

explanations.a: Not all funds are individually reported as major. GASB 34 provides a major fund identification framework — funds meeting size thresholds are reported individually; others are aggregated.
explanations.b: While the General Fund is always major, Enterprise Funds are major only if they meet the quantitative thresholds — being an Enterprise Fund alone does not make a fund major.
explanations.c: The Capital Projects Fund is not automatically major — it qualifies as major only if it meets the 10%/5% quantitative tests.
explanations.d: GASB 34 paragraph 76 requires major fund reporting as follows: (1) The General Fund is ALWAYS a major fund; (2) Other governmental funds and enterprise funds qualify as major if they meet both quantitative tests: (a) 10% of combined revenues, expenditures, assets, or liabilities of their fund type category AND (b) 5% of the same item for the aggregate of all governmental and enterprise funds combined; (3) Government officials may designate any fund as major even if it does not meet the quantitative criteria; (4) Funds that are not major are aggregated into 'Other Governmental Funds' or 'Other Enterprise Funds' columns — this provides detailed reporting for significant funds while preventing financial statement clutter from numerous small funds.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: SEC Form 8-K is required to be filed to

answers.text: Report audited annual financial results — the annual report with full financial statements
Register new securities before a public offering or major secondary offering
Report quarterly unaudited financial results — the quarterly earnings announcement
Report material current events requiring prompt public disclosure — such as executive departures, changes in auditors, bankruptcy filings, or material acquisitions

explanations.a: Audited annual financial results are reported on Form 10-K — the annual report. Form 8-K is for material current events, not scheduled annual reporting.
explanations.b: New securities registration uses Forms S-1 or S-3 — not Form 8-K. Registration statements are separate from periodic reporting.
explanations.c: Quarterly financial results are reported on Form 10-Q — the quarterly report. Form 8-K is not a periodic quarterly filing.
explanations.d: Form 8-K (Current Report) must be filed within four business days of specified triggering events. Common triggers include: Item 2.01 — completion of material acquisitions or dispositions; Item 4.01 — changes in registrant's certifying accountant; Item 5.02 — departure of directors or principal officers; Item 1.03 — bankruptcy or receivership; Item 7.01 — Regulation FD disclosure. The 8-K ensures timely disclosure of material events to all investors simultaneously.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company reports net income of $2,400,000. It has 600,000 weighted-average common shares outstanding and cumulative preferred stock with $120,000 of preferred dividends declared in the current year (plus $60,000 of prior-year dividends in arrears not declared in the current year). What is basic EPS?

answers.text: $3.80 — ($2,400,000 - $120,000 declared in current year) / 600,000 shares
$4.00 — $2,400,000 / 600,000, before preferred dividends

explanations.a: Basic EPS = (Net income - Preferred dividends on cumulative preferred declared in current period) / Weighted-average common shares. Only the $120,000 declared in the current year is deducted — prior-year arrears ($60,000) were already deducted from prior-period EPS and are not deducted again. Basic EPS = ($2,400,000 - $120,000) / 600,000 = $2,280,000 / 600,000 = $3.80.
explanations.b: Deducting $180,000 ($120,000 + $60,000 arrears) double-counts prior-period preferred dividends. ASC 260 deducts only the dividends on cumulative preferred that were declared or accrued in the current period — not cumulative amounts from prior periods already reflected in prior EPS calculations.
explanations.c: Basic EPS for common stockholders requires deducting preferred dividends. Cumulative preferred dividends reduce income available to common shareholders — omitting this deduction overstates basic EPS.
explanations.d: Deducting $300,000 does not correspond to any amount identifiable in the given information and produces an unsupported result.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company has 1,000,000 weighted-average common shares, net income of $3,000,000, and 100,000 in-the-money stock options with an exercise price of $20. The average market price during the year was $25. Under the treasury stock method, what is diluted share count?

answers.text: 1,100,000 — all 100,000 option shares added directly to the denominator
1,020,000 — 1,000,000 + net new shares from treasury stock method: [(100,000 options × $20 proceeds / $25 avg market price) subtracted from 100,000 exercised]
1,000,000 — options are out-of-the-money and excluded
1,080,000 — the 80,000 treasury shares purchased are added to the denominator

explanations.a: Adding all 100,000 option shares without the treasury stock offset overstates dilution — it ignores that proceeds from exercise are used to repurchase shares, partially offsetting the new shares issued.
explanations.b: Treasury stock method (ASC 260-10-45): Step 1 — Assume all in-the-money options are exercised: 100,000 × $20 = $2,000,000 proceeds. Step 2 — Use proceeds to repurchase at average market price: $2,000,000 / $25 = 80,000 shares. Step 3 — Net incremental shares: 100,000 exercised - 80,000 repurchased = 20,000 shares. Diluted denominator = 1,000,000 + 20,000 = 1,020,000. Exercise price ($20) < market price ($25), so options are in-the-money and dilutive.
explanations.c: Exercise price ($20) < average market price ($25) — the options ARE in-the-money and therefore dilutive. Options are excluded (antidilutive) only when exercise price exceeds average market price.
explanations.d: Adding 80,000 to the denominator is incorrect. 80,000 is the number of shares repurchased (subtracted from gross exercises) — it is not added. The NET addition is 100,000 - 80,000 = 20,000 incremental shares.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASC 280, an operating segment qualifies as a reportable segment if it exceeds ANY ONE of three 10% quantitative thresholds. These thresholds measure

answers.text: Number of employees, number of geographic locations, and product line count
Market capitalization, enterprise value, and free cash flow

Revenue (10% of all segments' combined revenues), absolute profit or loss (10% of the larger of: combined profits of profitable segments or combined losses of loss segments), and assets (10% of all segments' combined assets)
Headcount (10% of total), liabilities (10% of total), and revenue (10% of total)

explanations.a: Employee count and geographic locations are not the quantitative thresholds under ASC 280. Segment identification uses financial measures tied to the financial statements.
explanations.b: Market capitalization, enterprise value, and free cash flow are investor-focused metrics — not the ASC 280 quantitative thresholds.
explanations.c: ASC 280-10-50-12 establishes three quantitative thresholds for segment reporting: (1) Revenue — segment revenues (external + intersegment) ≥ 10% of combined revenues of all segments; (2) Profit or loss — the absolute value of the segment's reported profit or loss ≥ 10% of the greater of: (a) combined profit of all profitable segments, or (b) combined loss of all loss segments; (3) Assets — segment assets ≥ 10% of combined assets of all segments. A segment meeting any one threshold is a reportable segment. Additionally, all reportable segments must collectively represent at least 75% of external revenues — if not, additional segments are added until the 75% threshold is met.
explanations.d: Liabilities are not one of the three segment thresholds — assets are used. Headcount is also not a quantitative threshold under ASC 280.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under ASC 270 (Interim Financial Reporting), income tax expense in each interim period is computed using

answers.text: The actual tax liability for that specific quarter, calculated as if the quarter were a standalone annual period
A flat statutory rate applied to pre-tax income, ignoring permanent differences and tax credits
The prior year's effective tax rate, adjusted for any known changes
The estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date pre-tax income, with the cumulative tax expense adjusted each quarter as the estimate is refined

explanations.a: Treating each quarter as a standalone tax year (discrete method) creates volatility — a tax credit available only in Q2 would produce dramatically different tax rates across quarters. ASC 270 requires an integral approach for most items.
explanations.b: Using only the statutory rate ignores permanent differences, deductions, credits, and special rates that affect the company's actual tax burden — it would produce meaningfully incorrect interim tax amounts.
explanations.c: Using last year's ETR is not the required approach. The estimate should reflect current-year conditions and anticipated full-year tax consequences.
explanations.d: ASC 270-10-30-5 requires using an estimated annual effective tax rate (ETR) — an estimate of the full fiscal year's total tax expense divided by total pre-tax income. This ETR is applied to each quarter's cumulative year-to-date pre-tax income: Tax through current quarter = Year-to-date pre-tax income × Estimated annual ETR; Current quarter tax expense = Tax through current quarter - Tax recognized in prior quarters. The ETR estimate is updated each quarter as more information becomes available about full-year results, deductions, and credits.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company has 500,000 weighted-average common shares and net income of $1,500,000. It has 1,000 convertible bonds outstanding, each convertible into 50 shares. After-tax interest on the bonds for the year is $80,000. What is diluted EPS using the if-converted method?

answers.text: $2.87 — ($1,500,000 + $80,000) / (500,000 + 50,000) shares — basic EPS is $3.00 and this is dilutive
$3.00 — convertible bonds are always antidilutive for computing diluted EPS
$2.93 — $1,500,000 / (500,000 + 50,000) without adding back interest

explanations.a: If-converted method (ASC 260): (1) Numerator: add back after-tax interest savings — $1,500,000 + $80,000 = $1,580,000; (2) Denominator: add converted shares — 1,000 bonds × 50 shares = 50,000 new shares; 500,000 + 50,000 = 550,000; (3) Diluted EPS = $1,580,000 / 550,000 = $2.87. Since $2.87 < basic EPS of $3.00, these bonds are dilutive and included. The if-converted method tests whether including the securities reduces EPS — if yes, they are dilutive.
explanations.b: Convertible bonds are not always antidilutive. They are antidilutive only if their inclusion increases (rather than decreases) EPS. Here diluted EPS ($2.87) < basic EPS ($3.00) — the bonds are dilutive.
explanations.c: The after-tax interest is ADDED back to the numerator (not subtracted) — conversion eliminates the interest expense, increasing income available to common shareholders.
explanations.d: Omitting the interest add-back understates the numerator. When conversion is assumed under the if-converted method, the company avoids paying interest — that savings flows to income available to common shareholders.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company had 300,000 shares outstanding from January 1 through June 30. On July 1, it effected a 2-for-1 stock split. What is the weighted-average share count for the full year for EPS purposes?

answers.text: 600,000 — the split-adjusted share count is applied to the full year because stock splits are treated retroactively as if they occurred at the beginning of the earliest period presented
300,000 — the pre-split share count through June 30 and the post-split count are separately weighted and averaged at 225,000 + 150,000

explanations.a: Simple weighting of pre-split and post-split shares as if they represent two different periods creates inconsistency across periods. The retroactive treatment required by ASC 260 eliminates this problem.
explanations.b: This approach introduces an incorrect factor. The retroactive adjustment requires simply applying the split factor to all periods as if the split occurred at the start of the earliest period.
explanations.c: ASC 260-10-55-10 requires stock splits to be treated retroactively — applied to all share counts for all periods presented as if the split occurred at the beginning of the earliest period. For a 2-for-1 split on July 1: all pre-split shares (300,000) are multiplied by 2, making them 600,000 for the full year — no weighting of pre-split and post-split periods. Weighted-average = 600,000 shares for the full year. EPS for all comparative periods is also restated using the split-adjusted shares, ensuring comparability.
explanations.d: This approach (weighting pre-split and post-split periods separately) ignores the retroactive adjustment requirement. GAAP requires treating the split as if it occurred at the start of the year.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: An inventory write-down of $600,000 is recognized in Q2 due to a decline in net realizable value. By Q4, the inventory values recover and NRV exceeds original cost. Under ASC 270 (Interim Reporting), how should the Q4 recovery be handled?

answers.text: No recovery is recognized in Q4 — under both ASC 270 and ASC 330, once inventory is written down, the write-down establishes a new cost basis; US GAAP prohibits inventory write-ups
The full $600,000 is reversed in Q4 — ASC 270's integral view mandates full reversal of all within-year write-downs upon recovery
The recovery is deferred to the following fiscal year — interim write-downs are not reversed until the annual period closes
