ASC 270 permits recognizing a gain of up to the amount of the Q2 write-down if the recovery occurs within the same fiscal year — this is a specific exception to the general 'no write-up' rule that applies within an annual period for interim recoveries

explanations.a: While ASC 330 generally prohibits inventory write-ups above original cost for annual periods, ASC 270 contains a specific exception. If an inventory decline is recognized in an interim period and the decline is not considered permanent, a recovery within the same annual period may be recognized.
explanations.b: ASC 270-10-45-6 specifically provides that gains of up to the amount of losses recognized in earlier interim periods of the same annual period may be recognized. However, 'full reversal' is not automatic — the recovery gain cannot exceed the amount of the previously recognized write-down. If Q2 recognized a $600,000 write-down and Q4 values recover by $700,000 above original cost, only $600,000 can be recognized as a gain (not the additional $100,000 above original cost). The question says values recover and NRV exceeds original cost — so up to $600,000 can be reversed, which is the full write-down. This is a meaningful distinction from the annual reporting prohibition on write-ups.
explanations.c: Within-year interim write-downs have the specific recovery recognition provision under ASC 270 — the recovery is not deferred to the following year if it occurs within the current annual period.
explanations.d: This accurately describes the exception. ASC 270-10-45-6 is an exception to the general prohibition on inventory write-ups — within the same fiscal year, if inventory values recover after an interim write-down, a gain (up to the previously recognized write-down) may be recognized in the subsequent interim period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Under the cash basis of accounting, revenue and expenses are recognized when

answers.text: Revenue is earned; expenses are incurred — the same principles as GAAP accrual
Cash is received (for revenue) and cash is paid (for expenses) — regardless of when related goods or services are delivered or consumed
Billing occurs (for revenue) and purchase orders are issued (for expenses)
Contracts are signed (for revenue) and commitments are made (for expenses)

explanations.a: Revenue earned and expenses incurred describes accrual basis (GAAP) — not cash basis. The cash basis specifically departs from GAAP by tying recognition entirely to cash flows.
explanations.b: The cash basis recognizes revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid — regardless of when economic activity (delivery of goods, rendering of services, consumption of resources) occurs. This produces statements that closely mirror actual cash transactions and is used by many small businesses, professionals, and individuals for both reporting and tax purposes.
explanations.c: Billing dates and purchase order issuance are neither cash basis nor full accrual — they represent specific billing/commitment triggers that don't define either framework.
explanations.d: Contract signing represents the commitment stage — before either cash receipt or service delivery. Neither contract signing nor commitment issuance is the trigger for cash basis recognition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A company prepares tax-basis financial statements. Which of the following statements BEST describes what this means?

answers.text: The statements use GAAP for revenue recognition but apply MACRS depreciation for all fixed assets
The statements follow modified accrual — the same basis as governmental funds

The statements apply all recognition, measurement, and disclosure principles consistent with the income tax return — including MACRS depreciation, installment method election (if applicable), and other tax-specific treatments — not GAAP
The statements present the same results as GAAP because US entities must conform book and tax accounting

explanations.a: Tax-basis statements use ALL income tax accounting principles, not just MACRS depreciation. Applying only depreciation on a tax basis while retaining GAAP revenue recognition would be a partial approach — not a complete tax-basis framework.
explanations.b: Modified accrual is a government accounting term — it describes the basis used for governmental funds under GASB standards. The income tax basis is a different special-purpose framework not related to modified accrual.
explanations.c: Financial statements prepared on the income tax basis apply all the accounting treatments required or permitted by the income tax code and regulations — including: MACRS accelerated depreciation and Section 179 expensing; installment method revenue recognition (when elected); bad debt deductions using the specific charge-off method; income inclusion/exclusion rules; and other tax-specific provisions. Tax-basis net income equals taxable income (or tracks it closely), which differs from GAAP income primarily because of timing differences (depreciation) and permanent differences.
explanations.d: US GAAP and income tax accounting are separate frameworks. There is no general requirement for book-tax conformity — many companies maintain two separate sets of accounting records. The resulting differences give rise to deferred tax assets and liabilities in GAAP financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A service company earned $800,000 in revenues but collected only $650,000 in cash. It incurred $500,000 in expenses but paid only $400,000. What is cash-basis income for the year?

answers.text: $250,000 — cash receipts ($650,000) minus cash payments ($400,000)
$300,000 — revenues earned ($800,000) minus expenses incurred ($500,000) — the GAAP accrual result
$400,000 — the difference in amounts billed versus amounts paid
$150,000 — the excess of revenue over expenses for the cash-basis subset

explanations.a: Under the cash basis, only actual cash flows are recognized: Revenue = Cash received = $650,000; Expenses = Cash paid = $400,000; Cash-basis income = $650,000 - $400,000 = $250,000. The uncollected revenue ($150,000) and unpaid expenses ($100,000) are ignored — cash basis excludes receivables and payables.
explanations.b: $300,000 is the GAAP accrual result ($800,000 earned - $500,000 incurred). This uses revenue when earned and expense when incurred — full accrual, not cash basis.
explanations.c: $400,000 does not correspond to a recognized calculation for cash-basis income from the given data.
explanations.d: $150,000 does not correspond to a valid cash-basis calculation. Cash-basis income is $250,000 (cash received minus cash paid).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: Statutory Accounting Principles (SAP) used by insurance companies to prepare statutory financial statements represent which type of special-purpose framework?

answers.text: Tax basis — insurance statutory accounting follows IRS regulations
Cash basis — insurance companies use cash recognition due to claim uncertainty
Contractual basis — SAP is established by the insurance policies between insurers and policyholders
Regulatory basis — SAP is prescribed by state insurance regulators primarily to assess insurer solvency, and differs materially from GAAP in several respects

explanations.a: SAP is not established by the IRS or income tax regulations. It is prescribed by state insurance departments through NAIC model laws and is focused on solvency, not income tax measurement.
explanations.b: SAP is not a cash basis. It uses accrual concepts but applies them more conservatively than GAAP — requiring immediate expensing of policyholder acquisition costs and more conservative asset valuations.
explanations.c: SAP is not defined by individual insurance contracts — it is mandated by state insurance regulatory authorities for all insurers doing business in that state.
explanations.d: Statutory Accounting Principles represent a regulatory-basis special-purpose framework. State insurance regulators (following NAIC standards) require insurers to prepare statutory financial statements — filed with state departments of insurance — using SAP rather than GAAP. Key differences from GAAP: (1) policyholder acquisition costs are immediately expensed (GAAP defers and amortizes them); (2) certain assets are 'non-admitted' (excluded from the statutory balance sheet); (3) investment valuations use different standards; (4) statutory surplus differs from GAAP equity. The regulatory objective is solvency assessment — ensuring insurers can pay future claims.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: In the early years of a depreciable asset's life, how does tax-basis net income typically compare to GAAP net income for entities using MACRS for tax and straight-line for GAAP?

answers.text: Tax-basis income is HIGHER than GAAP in early years — accelerated MACRS produces lower depreciation charges than straight-line

Tax-basis income is LOWER than GAAP in early years because MACRS accelerated depreciation exceeds straight-line GAAP depreciation, creating higher tax-basis expenses; this relationship reverses in later years when MACRS falls below straight-line
Tax-basis and GAAP income are identical — US GAAP and income tax must be consistent for depreciable assets
Tax-basis income is HIGHER in early years because MACRS creates tax deductions that are not recognized as expenses in GAAP statements

explanations.a: MACRS produces HIGHER (accelerated, front-loaded) depreciation in early years — not lower. This results in lower tax-basis income, not higher.
explanations.b: MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System) front-loads depreciation deductions — in early years of an asset's life, MACRS depreciation significantly exceeds straight-line GAAP depreciation. For example, 5-year MACRS Year 2 is 32% of cost vs. 20% straight-line. The higher depreciation reduces tax-basis income below GAAP income. In later years, MACRS depreciation falls below straight-line — so tax-basis income recovers above GAAP income. The total depreciation over the asset's full life is the same under both methods (the cost minus salvage value), just accelerated under MACRS.
explanations.c: GAAP and income tax depreciation frequently differ — this is one of the primary sources of deferred tax liabilities. There is no conformity requirement.
explanations.d: MACRS produces higher (not lower) tax-basis depreciation in early years, creating LOWER (not higher) tax-basis income. Higher deductions reduce income — they do not increase it.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A 'modified cash basis' of accounting differs from both pure cash basis and full accrual (GAAP) in that the modified cash basis

answers.text: Is identical to GAAP except for depreciation — the 'modification' refers only to accelerated depreciation methods
Uses the same principles as governmental modified accrual — recognizing revenues when measurable and available
Is a formally defined basis codified in ASC with specific rules governing which modifications are permitted

Applies cash-basis principles for most items but introduces certain accruals — such as recording accounts receivable for significant year-end revenue or accounts payable for major obligations — that make the statements more useful while retaining overall cash-basis simplicity

explanations.a: Modified cash basis does not simply apply GAAP with accelerated depreciation. The modifications relate to selected accruals for significant items — not only to depreciation methods.
explanations.b: Governmental modified accrual is a separate, specifically defined basis under GASB standards with distinct rules about availability windows. The 'modified cash basis' used by small businesses is a different concept with different modifications.
explanations.c: Modified cash basis is not a formally codified standard — it is a practical adaptation of cash basis accounting that incorporates selected accruals to improve statement usefulness. There is no single ASC section that defines the specific modifications permitted.
explanations.d: The modified cash basis (sometimes called 'modified accrual' informally in non-governmental contexts, though this terminology can create confusion with GASB standards) is a practical hybrid: it starts with cash-basis simplicity but incorporates certain significant accruals — such as recognizing accounts receivable for material year-end billings, recording accounts payable for significant year-end obligations, or capitalizing and depreciating major fixed assets. These modifications improve statement utility without adopting full GAAP accrual complexity. The resulting statements are easier and less expensive to prepare than GAAP while providing more economic accuracy than pure cash basis.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: A partnership agreement specifies that the partnership's financial results are to be measured using specific accounting rules defined in the partnership agreement — including recognizing income on a completed-contract basis and valuing certain assets at historical cost without impairment testing. These financial statements use a

answers.text: Tax basis — partnership income allocation follows tax principles
Cash basis — the partnership is avoiding accrual accounting through agreement-based rules
Contractual basis — a special-purpose framework defined by the specific terms of a contract or agreement, designed to serve the needs of the parties to that agreement
Regulatory basis — partnership agreements must conform to state partnership statutes that prescribe accounting methods

explanations.a: Tax basis follows income tax law, not a partnership agreement. If the partnership agreement specified using tax code rules (MACRS depreciation, tax revenue recognition), it could overlap with tax basis — but the agreement-defined basis described here with completed-contract and no impairment testing is not a standard tax-basis element.
explanations.b: Completed-contract basis and historical cost without impairment testing are not characteristics of cash basis accounting. Cash basis recognizes only cash receipts and payments — it is independent of revenue recognition methods like completed-contract.
explanations.c: A contractual basis (one of the four types of special-purpose frameworks under ASU 2016-14) is a financial reporting framework that follows the requirements of a contractual arrangement — such as a partnership agreement, loan agreement, or joint venture agreement. The parties to the agreement define the measurement and recognition rules to serve their specific needs. In this case, the partnership agreement specifies completed-contract revenue recognition and historical cost without impairment, which may differ materially from GAAP — but serves the partners' specific objectives for understanding the partnership's performance.
explanations.d: State partnership statutes generally do not prescribe specific accounting methods for partnership financial statements — they address legal formation, liability, and governance. Partnership accounting is typically governed by GAAP or an agreement-defined basis, not by regulatory prescription.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.text: When an auditor reports on financial statements prepared on the income tax basis (a special-purpose framework), the audit report must include which additional element not present in a standard GAAP audit report?

answers.text: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph that identifies the income tax basis, refers to the note describing the basis, and states that the basis may differ from GAAP in material respects — communicating to users that different accounting principles apply
A qualified opinion — tax-basis financial statements always require a qualified opinion because they depart from GAAP
A disclaimer of opinion — the auditor cannot form an opinion on statements not prepared on GAAP
No additional elements — a standard unmodified audit report is issued without any modification for tax-basis statements

explanations.a: AU-C Section 800 requires that when auditing special-purpose framework financial statements, the auditor's report must include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that: (1) identifies the basis of accounting used (income tax basis); (2) refers to the note in the financial statements that describes the basis; and (3) for cash basis and tax basis statements, includes a statement that the basis differs from GAAP. This paragraph alerts users — who may be accustomed to GAAP financial statements — that different principles apply. The paragraph does not modify the audit opinion (which remains unmodified if the statements are fairly presented in accordance with the tax basis) but supplements it with essential context.
explanations.b: An unmodified opinion is appropriate for tax-basis statements that are fairly presented in accordance with tax principles. A qualified opinion would imply a misstatement or scope limitation — not merely the use of a different framework.
explanations.c: A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor cannot form any opinion. Auditors regularly audit and opine on special-purpose framework statements — the basis of accounting used does not prevent forming an opinion.
explanations.d: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph IS required by AU-C 800 for SPF audits — the audit report is not identical to a standard GAAP report. The emphasis-of-matter paragraph is the required addition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: The current ratio is calculated as

answers.text: Current assets divided by current liabilities — measuring the entity's ability to pay short-term obligations with its short-term assets
Total assets divided by total liabilities — measuring overall financial leverage
Net income divided by average stockholders' equity — measuring return on equity
Cash and equivalents divided by current liabilities — the strictest measure of liquidity

explanations.a: The current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities. It measures whether the company has sufficient short-term assets to cover its short-term obligations. A ratio above 1.0 means current assets exceed current liabilities. A ratio of 2.0 is often cited as a benchmark but varies significantly by industry — capital-intensive manufacturers may comfortably operate with lower ratios while retailers typically need higher ratios.
explanations.b: Total assets / Total liabilities measures the degree to which assets are financed by debt — this is related to financial leverage, not the current ratio.
explanations.c: Net income / Average stockholders' equity is the formula for Return on Equity (ROE) — a profitability measure, not a liquidity ratio.
explanations.d: Cash and equivalents / Current liabilities is the cash ratio — the most conservative liquidity measure, more restrictive than the current ratio because it excludes receivables and inventory.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: Company A has the following balance sheet items: cash $50,000; accounts receivable $150,000; inventory $200,000; prepaid expenses $30,000; and current liabilities of $200,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?

answers.text: 1.00 — ($50,000 + $150,000 + $0) / $200,000, excluding inventory and prepaids from the quick assets

explanations.a: This includes inventory and prepaid expenses in the quick ratio — both are excluded because they are less liquid. Including them would produce the current ratio, not the quick ratio.
explanations.b: This arrives at 1.00 as well but presents the calculation as ($50,000 + $150,000) / $200,000 = 1.00 — this is actually correct math and produces the same result as option d, but the presentation in option b doesn't make the zero for prepaids explicit.
explanations.c: Including prepaid expenses ($30,000) in the quick ratio is incorrect. Prepaid expenses are excluded from the quick ratio because they represent already-paid future expenses — they cannot be quickly converted to cash.
explanations.d: The quick (acid-test) ratio = (Cash + Short-term investments + Net accounts receivable) / Current liabilities. It excludes inventory (which may not sell quickly) and prepaid expenses (which have no cash-conversion value). Quick assets = $50,000 (cash) + $150,000 (receivables) = $200,000. Quick ratio = $200,000 / $200,000 = 1.00. This means the company has exactly enough liquid assets to cover current liabilities without relying on inventory liquidation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: A company had average accounts receivable of $500,000 and net credit sales of $3,650,000 for the year. What is the days sales outstanding (DSO)?

answers.text: 7.3 times (the AR turnover) — DSO is the same as the AR turnover ratio
100 days — $3,650,000 / $500,000 × 365 (calculated incorrectly with receivables in denominator)

explanations.a: This calculation = ($500,000 / $3,650,000) × 365 = 0.137 × 365 = 50 days. The math happens to give the same answer as option b because both approaches yield the same result when done correctly: DSO = (Avg AR / Net sales) × 365 = ($500,000 / $3,650,000) × 365 = 50 days. Options a and b are mathematically equivalent — both give 50 days.
explanations.b: Days Sales Outstanding = Average AR / (Net credit sales / 365) = $500,000 / ($3,650,000 / 365) = $500,000 / $10,000 per day = 50 days. DSO measures the average number of days it takes to collect credit sales — 50 days means customers take, on average, 50 days to pay. AR Turnover = $3,650,000 / $500,000 = 7.3 times; DSO = 365 / 7.3 = 50 days. Both calculation methods produce 50 days.
explanations.c: DSO and AR turnover are different metrics — they are reciprocally related (DSO = 365 / AR turnover), but DSO measures days and AR turnover measures times per year. Saying they are the same is incorrect.
explanations.d: Inverting the formula places receivables in the denominator of the turnover calculation instead of the numerator, producing an inverted AR turnover rate — not DSO.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: Company B has net income of $400,000, beginning stockholders' equity of $2,000,000, and ending stockholders' equity of $2,200,000. What is return on equity (ROE)?

answers.text: 18.2% — $400,000 / $2,200,000 (using ending equity only)
20.0% — $400,000 / $2,000,000 (using beginning equity only)
16.7% — $400,000 / ($2,400,000), using the sum of beginning and ending equity without averaging

explanations.a: Using only ending equity ignores the starting point of the period. Since net income is earned over the course of the year, the appropriate denominator is the average equity that was at risk during the period.
explanations.b: Using only beginning equity ignores the equity generated during the year (net income and other additions). Average equity is the standard denominator for ROE.
explanations.c: ROE = Net income / Average stockholders' equity. Average equity = ($2,000,000 + $2,200,000) / 2 = $2,100,000. ROE = $400,000 / $2,100,000 = 19.05%, approximately 19.0%. Using average equity is the standard approach because it reflects the equity base that generated the return throughout the period — not just the beginning or ending balance.
explanations.d: Dividing by the sum of beginning and ending equity without dividing by 2 would halve the ROE — producing a denominator twice as large as the correct average equity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: The DuPont analysis decomposes return on equity (ROE) into which three components?

answers.text: Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier (financial leverage) — allowing analysis of whether ROE changes are driven by profitability, efficiency, or leverage
Gross margin × Operating margin × Net margin — three layers of profitability analysis
Current ratio × Quick ratio × Cash ratio — three measures of liquidity driving equity returns
Return on assets × Asset growth × Equity issuances — three drivers of equity value

explanations.a: The DuPont decomposition expresses ROE as: ROE = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier — where: (1) Net profit margin = Net income / Net sales (profitability — how much of each dollar of sales becomes income); (2) Asset turnover = Net sales / Average total assets (efficiency — how effectively assets are used to generate sales); (3) Equity multiplier = Average total assets / Average stockholders' equity (financial leverage — how much assets are financed by equity vs. debt). This framework allows analysts to diagnose the source of ROE changes — a declining ROE may reflect lower margins, less efficient asset use, or reduced leverage.
explanations.b: Gross margin, operating margin, and net margin are all profitability ratios — they do not capture the efficiency and leverage dimensions that DuPont analysis is designed to reveal.
explanations.c: Current, quick, and cash ratios are liquidity measures — they have no direct mathematical connection to ROE decomposition.
explanations.d: ROA, asset growth, and equity issuances do not constitute the standard DuPont decomposition framework.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Financial Accounting and Reporting
questions.name: Financial Reporting
questions.keyword: financial statement ratios and performance metrics
questions.text: A company has EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) of $800,000 and interest expense of $200,000. Its times interest earned (TIE) ratio is 4.0. If interest expense increases to $320,000 (and EBIT remains unchanged), which assessment is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: The TIE improves to 6.0 — higher interest indicates more financial strength
The TIE remains at 4.0 — TIE is insensitive to changes in interest expense
The TIE deteriorates to 2.5, indicating reduced ability to service debt from operating earnings — this may concern lenders monitoring debt covenant compliance
The TIE cannot be calculated without knowing the tax rate — income taxes must be excluded from the calculation

explanations.a: A higher interest expense reduces the TIE ratio — it does not improve it. Higher interest payments mean the company must generate more operating income to cover its obligations, reducing the coverage cushion.
explanations.b: TIE is directly affected by changes in interest expense — as the denominator increases, the ratio falls. TIE = EBIT / Interest expense; as interest increases, TIE decreases.
explanations.c: Original TIE = $800,000 / $200,000 = 4.0. New TIE = $800,000 / $320,000 = 2.5. The ratio falls from 4.0 to 2.5, meaning the company's operating income now covers interest expenses only 2.5 times rather than 4.0 times. A lower TIE signals increased financial risk — lenders and bondholders use the TIE as a key measure of debt service capacity, and debt covenants often specify minimum TIE requirements. A TIE of 2.5 may approach or breach covenant thresholds.
explanations.d: TIE uses EBIT — which already excludes income taxes (by definition, EBIT is before both interest and taxes). No tax rate information is needed to calculate TIE.

questions.text: A retail company's inventory turnover ratio declined from 8.0 times to 5.0 times year over year, while industry average inventory turnover is 9.0 times. What does this trend MOST likely indicate?

answers.text: Improved inventory management — higher remaining inventory means the company has more safety stock
More efficient purchasing — lower turnover means the company is buying less frequently and saving on order costs
Improved gross margins — slower inventory turnover results from selling at higher prices

Potentially slow-moving, excess, or obsolete inventory — lower-than-industry turnover suggests inventory is moving slowly, which can indicate demand weakness, overstocking, or product obsolescence, and ties up cash while increasing obsolescence risk

explanations.a: A high inventory turnover (fast movement) indicates efficient inventory management. A low turnover ratio indicates the opposite — inventory is sitting longer than necessary or industry norms.
explanations.b: Lower inventory turnover is not a sign of purchasing efficiency. Efficient purchasing aims to minimize excess inventory while meeting demand — purchasing less frequently (and holding more inventory longer) increases carrying costs and obsolescence risk.
explanations.c: Gross margin improvement is not directly caused by lower inventory turnover. Margins reflect selling price relative to cost — not how quickly inventory moves.
explanations.d: Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average inventory. A decline from 8.0 to 5.0 (against an industry average of 9.0) means inventory is taking significantly longer to sell. This pattern is associated with: (1) declining demand for the company's products; (2) overpurchasing or overproduction creating excess inventory; (3) product obsolescence or quality issues preventing sales at normal prices; and (4) competitive pressures reducing the company's sales velocity. Slow-moving inventory ties up working capital, increases storage and insurance costs, and raises the risk of markdowns or write-offs — all of which erode profitability.

questions.text: A company has total stockholders' equity of $5,000,000 and 1,000,000 common shares outstanding. Its stock trades at $12 per share. What is the book value per share, and what does the comparison to market price suggest?

answers.text: Book value per share = $12.00 — book and market values are always the same for correctly priced stocks

Book value per share = $5.00; market price ($12) significantly exceeds book value — suggesting the market expects future earnings and growth beyond what historical cost accounting captures, or the company has significant unrecognized intangible assets
Book value per share = $12.00 — book value per share equals the current market price by definition
Book value per share = $5.00 — the Price-to-Book ratio of 2.4× indicates the market undervalues the stock

explanations.a: Book value and market value are equal only by coincidence — they represent fundamentally different concepts. Book value reflects historical cost accounting; market value reflects investor expectations about future cash flows.
explanations.b: Book value per share = Total stockholders' equity / Common shares outstanding = $5,000,000 / 1,000,000 = $5.00 per share. Market price is $12.00 per share. The Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio = $12 / $5 = 2.4×. Market price exceeding book value typically indicates: (1) the market expects the company to generate returns above its cost of capital; (2) the company has valuable assets not captured in historical cost accounting — such as brand value, customer relationships, patents, or proprietary technology; (3) investor confidence in future earnings growth. A P/B above 1.0 is common for successful companies with strong intangibles or high return on equity.
explanations.c: Book value and market price are different concepts — they are equal only when a company's market capitalization equals the book value of its equity, which is uncommon.
explanations.d: A P/B ratio of 2.4× does not indicate undervaluation — it suggests the market values the company above book value, which typically reflects positive expectations. Undervaluation would be suggested by a P/B ratio below 1.0 (market price below book value).
